item.title: Sitemap 'Couldn't fetch' for 10 days in GSC – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Search Console showed 'Couldn't fetch' for ten days; a new domain property processed the same sitemaps in seconds

Behind the 'Couldn't fetch' label the API said isPending=True with no lastDownloaded. For those ten days, almost every page that got indexed was one we had requested by hand.

Getting this site indexed 2/3

When Google Search Console's sitemap report says 'Couldn't fetch', most people suspect the file format or the server first. Here it was neither: Google simply had not downloaded the file even once. We submitted sitemap.xml to Search Console, and Google never fetched it in the ten days before the site moved. It was first submitted on October 21, 2026 (API date). On October 25 a live URL test fetched the same file without trouble, and Bing processed our sitemap.xml that same day. On October 31 the site moved to its own domain; we submitted the same four sitemaps to a new domain property, and Google downloaded all four within seven seconds of submission.

Old property: still pending on November 1. New property: seconds

On the morning of November 1 we read both properties' sitemap lists again. The URL-prefix property for the old github.io address still lists sitemap.xml and its three child sitemaps as isPending=True, no lastDownloaded, errors=0. All four were last submitted on October 30 (sitemap.xml at 03:43, the children at 15:43). In the new domain property the same four read isPending=False, errors=0, with lastDownloaded between 17:05:08 and 17:05:14 on October 31. They were submitted at 17:05:07 to 17:05:08, so all four were downloaded within seven seconds (the fastest in under one second).

The move rewrote the old address to the new domain across the site; the sitemap layout (one index, three children) and the rules that generate it did not change. Every old URL redirects with a single 301 to the same path on the new domain, and the audit run against the new domain found all 196 URLs returning 200 with self-referencing canonicals. Eleven hours after the move, a full URL Inspection run in the new property (198 URLs) showed 114 as 'Discovered - currently not indexed'.

Googlebot fetched the file in a live test

On the afternoon of October 25 the operator pointed out that the sitemap wasn't showing up in Search Console and that robots.txt seemed to be missing. The agent found that robots.txt returned 200 with Allow: / and a Sitemap line. sitemap.xml was a standard sitemaps.org 0.9 urlset with the hreflang and image extensions; it rendered as a table in the browser only because of an xml-stylesheet meant for people. The audit script opened all 154 URLs: every one returned 200 with a self canonical, no noindex, reciprocal hreflang and valid lastmod, and all 261 images returned 200.

At 14:38 we ran the live URL test in URL Inspection on the sitemap.xml address. Googlebot fetched it and reported that the URL was available to Google. That afternoon the Sitemaps report said 'Couldn't fetch', and the API said isPending=True, no lastDownloaded, 0 errors. There was no record of a fetch attempt at all.

New format, four resubmissions, child sitemaps: still pending

The operator suspected the structure, so around 17:00 the agent turned sitemap.xml into a plain sitemapindex (three commits). The three child sitemaps keep only loc, lastmod, priority and changefreq; the XSL, hreflang and image tags were removed. lastmod follows the rule in our note on setting sitemap lastmod from a content hash. We also added an HTML site map, which puts all 156 URLs within two clicks of the home page. In the same hour the operator added the site to Bing Webmaster Tools by importing it from Search Console. Bing fetched the new sitemap.xml that day, marked it Success and found the three child sitemaps. Google was still pending that evening.

We resubmitted sitemap.xml through the API twice on October 25 and once each on October 27 and in the early hours of October 30, and got 204 every time. On the afternoon of October 30 the API reported sitemap.xml as isSitemapsIndex=False: Google had never downloaded it, so it did not even know the file was an index. If only the first pass through an index were slow, a child sitemap should get processed first, so we submitted the three children directly (94, 44 and 48 URLs). All four stayed pending.

The agent's first note, on the morning of October 25, called the state "a normal delay for a new property" and proposed waiting a week; the old property was still pending on November 1. When it resubmitted on October 25 it also resubmitted rss.xml and en/rss.xml as sitemaps, which breaks this site's own rule that RSS feeds are never submitted as sitemaps, and it submitted sitemap.xml?v=20261025 as a separate duplicate. The duplicate was deleted at around 17:00 that day; the two feeds were deleted with the operator's approval, leaving sitemap.xml alone.

When you see 'Couldn't fetch', don't start by rewriting the file. Check lastDownloaded in the API and run the live URL test first. On this site, with lastDownloaded empty and the live test passing, changing the format did not end the wait.

Host, property type and submission date all changed at once

URLs we requested by hand were mostly crawled within one to four hours, so Googlebot could reach the site. The explanation that remains is that the property's sitemap never reached the front of Google's processing queue; we could not confirm that, because Google does not show why. Google's Sitemaps report help lists five causes of 'Couldn't fetch': a robots.txt block, an unresolved manual action, a 404, a general error such as an unavailable server, and low crawl demand for the sitemap. Of the first four, we ruled out the robots block, the 404 and server errors above; we did not check the Manual actions report (the URLs we requested were indexed within hours). Low crawl demand stays a hypothesis we cannot check.

Three things changed at once with the new property: the host went from github.io to our own domain, the property type went from URL prefix to a domain property verified by DNS TXT, and the submission came ten days later. This observation cannot separate the three, so this note does not name github.io as the cause.

While the sitemap had never been read, URL Inspection in the old property still showed coverageState as 'Submitted and indexed' (the October 25 full run, and again on November 1). On this site, 'Submitted' did not mean the sitemap had been processed.

For ten days, indexing grew mostly through manual requests

The full URL Inspection run on the morning of October 25 found 7 of 148 URLs indexed (4.7%) and 141 as 'URL is unknown to Google'. That day the operator handed Search Console write tasks to the agent, which started requesting indexing in the Search Console UI. At 14:29 an API check showed 7 of 10 requested URLs as 'Submitted and indexed', one to two hours after the requests. URLs we had not requested stayed where they were: the 03:00 run on October 26 still counted 22 indexed, the same as the previous afternoon, and 133 unknown.

From then on we requested new notes and a queue every day. The indexed count went to 44 (October 27), 73 (October 28), 146 (October 30) and 162 (October 31). The October 27 run showed nearly every requested URL indexed and most unrequested ones unknown. A few notes stayed unknown even after several requests.

The agent misread the request limit at first. On October 25 a 'Quota exceeded' message appeared after 15 accepted requests, and it wrote down "15 to 16 per day". On October 27 forty requests went through without that message. On October 29, 49 clicks produced 44 accepted requests; 'Quota exceeded' appeared five times in between, and each time the very next request was accepted. We now read it as a short-interval rate limit. These are observations from one property, not limits Google has published. Driving the UI from a browser took about two and a half minutes per request.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

After the move, 5 of 7 requests indexed within four hours

The domain move had been decided for reasons unrelated to the sitemap, and it happened at 17:00 on October 31. New URLs showed up as 'Discovered - currently not indexed' within minutes, and the home page was indexed at its new address three hours after the move. From 19:47 we requested the seven pages that had impressions in the old property; four hours later five were 'Submitted and indexed'. That request-to-index time is about what we saw in the old property (one to four hours).

One of the seven, /ax/hwp-viewer-rhwp-webview/, came back as 'Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user'. Inspecting the old URL in the old property showed 'Submitted and indexed', with the old URL itself as Google's canonical and a last crawl on October 27, before the 301 existed. The 03:00 full run in the new property on November 1 found 10 such Duplicate pages, many of them pages that had impressions in the old property. On the morning of November 1 we inspected five of them again: all five were still Duplicate, and googleCanonical was empty for three and showed the github.io URL for two.

For Duplicate pages we request indexing for the old URL in the old property. The new address has already been crawled and the old URL is still the canonical, so we expect the canonical to move only after Google recrawls the old URL and sees the 301. We sent one such request on the night of October 31 and ten on the morning of November 1.

The new property still had zero rows of search performance data on the morning of November 1, and as of that morning the old property's last daily row was October 29, with 84 impressions, its highest day until then. Search performance data usually lands two to three days late, so this cannot yet be told apart from reporting lag.

For Google, only the UI indexing request was left

We waited ten days, but with six new pages (Korean and English) going out every day we could not wait another week. The Indexing API covers only job postings and livestream video pages, so our notes don't qualify. IndexNow pings went out with every publish, but its receivers are engines such as Bing and Naver (Korea's largest portal); Google does not use it. That left the URL Inspection indexing request, which only exists in the UI, so the agent drove it through a browser.

If lastDownloaded is set, this is a different problem

If lastDownloaded has a value and errors is above zero, Google downloaded the file and failed while reading it; fix the reported errors. If the live URL test fails with a 404, a robots block or a redirect, the fetch is really failing. This is one site and two properties, so we can't say whether other sites on github.io see the same wait.

What to check when a sitemap says 'Couldn't fetch'

  1. Read the sitemap list from the Search Console API and look at isPending, lastDownloaded, errors, isSitemapsIndex and lastSubmitted. No lastDownloaded and zero errors means Google has never downloaded it; the live test in the next step tells pending from failure.
  2. Run the live URL test in URL Inspection on the sitemap.xml address. If it says the URL is available to Google, fetching works.
  3. Open every URL in the sitemap and confirm 200, a self canonical, no noindex, reciprocal hreflang and valid lastmod.
  4. Submit the same sitemap to Bing Webmaster Tools. If Bing processes it, that is one more sign the file's format and access are fine.
  5. If it is pending, request indexing for every new page. On 'Quota exceeded', retry the same URL a little later.
  6. Once a day, run URL Inspection over every URL and record coverageState and lastCrawlTime.
  7. After a domain move, take the Duplicate pages in the new property and request indexing for their old URLs in the old property.
# sitemap status (read only)
GET https://www.googleapis.com/webmasters/v3/sites/<property>/sitemaps
  → path, isPending, lastDownloaded, isSitemapsIndex, errors, lastSubmitted
# index status of one URL
POST https://searchconsole.googleapis.com/v1/urlInspection/index:inspect
  {"inspectionUrl": "<URL>", "siteUrl": "<property>"}
  → coverageState, lastCrawlTime, googleCanonical
# <property>: URL prefix https://example.github.io/ (URL-encoded), domain property sc-domain:example.com

Ten Duplicate pages and four old sitemaps

On the morning of November 1 the old URL /ax/hwp-viewer-rhwp-webview/ still had October 27 as its last crawl. The next URL Inspection run will show whether the ten old-property requests sent that morning get the 301 read. We are also watching whether the old property's four sitemaps ever get processed, and whether daily rows from October 30 on show up in the old property.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Getting this site indexed: all 3 parts

  1. Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash
  2. Structured data after FAQ rich results ended: what we kept for GEO

FAQ

Does 'Couldn't fetch' in the Search Console Sitemaps report mean the file is broken?

Not on this site. The API said isPending=True, no lastDownloaded and zero errors, and the live URL test fetched the file.

If the sitemap is never processed, do new pages get indexed?

Requesting indexing by hand worked. During the ten pending days most requested URLs were indexed within one to four hours.

Does moving from github.io to a custom domain get the sitemap processed right away?

For this site Google downloaded it within seven seconds of submission. That is one observation in which the host, the property type and the submission date all changed together.

Sources: Search Console API reads (sitemaps, URL Inspection), the sitemap audit script's output, Bing Webmaster Tools screens and the site's git history. Times are KST (UTC+9), as of November 1, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Android 16 KB page size: add the linker flag before you upgrade the NDK (NDK 27 and 29 tinted our photos blue)
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

item.title: Interstitial ad frequency: tutorials don't count – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

We set interstitial frequency from device timelines, and tutorials don't count

Once the three tutorial puzzles stopped counting toward ads, the first interstitial in puzzle mode moved to after the third real puzzle. We chose what to count by reading ad logs from fresh installs in time order.

Ads and metrics for two puzzle games 2/4

Free games earn from interstitials between rounds, but a new player who sees an ad before they understand the game tends to leave. So games add guard rules such as "no interstitial in the first three runs or the first 90 seconds". What those rules do in practice is hard to tell from the spec alone.

On October 4, 2026 we let a script play a fresh install of Block Turn at human pace on a Galaxy S21 and lined up the ad log by time. The first interstitial came 91 seconds after launch, before a single real puzzle: the three tutorial puzzles had already satisfied the three-run rule. Once tutorials stopped counting, the emulator's first interstitial moved from 181 s to 314 s, and the slower classic mode now counts a game over as two runs.

On a fresh install, the first interstitial came before any real puzzle

Block Turn shows an interstitial only when a player taps Next, Play again or Home after a finished run. The numbers lived in one place in the code: at least 3 finished runs, 2 runs since the last interstitial, 90 s since the session started, 120 s since the previous full-screen ad, at most 5 per session and 20 per day, and only if an ad was already loaded. Here "full-screen ad" means interstitials, rewarded ads and app open ads together. The PRD (v2.1 §11.2) rules out an interstitial within the first three finished runs and the first 90 seconds of a session, and hides the banner on the tutorial puzzles and the first three runs.

Every run on October 4 started from cleared app data. The session script plays scripted runs, or personas, each with a fixed mode and pace range, and reads ad impressions from the SDK log. On the S21, the first interstitial came at 91 s, on Next after tutorial R003. The emulator finished the tutorials in 64 s; its first interstitial came after R004, at 181 s. Two other emulator personas (mixed and return) got their first one at 158 s and 134 s.

The three tutorials had already met the 3-run gate

The function that counted finished runs did not tell tutorials apart. In the first version of the app, written with the coding agent, the run-end function added every tutorial solve to the banner's run count and to the interstitial's win count, exactly like a real run. By the time the third tutorial ended, "3 finished runs" was already true.

Both the 3-run gate and the 90-second grace were meant to protect a new player. The three tutorials take 64 to 90 seconds, so the two guards opened at nearly the same time instead of adding up. The first ad's timing then depended on how fast the tutorials were cleared. The emulator met the 3-run gate at 64 s but was still inside the 90-second grace, so its ad waited for the next run, R004; on the S21 the grace was nearly over when R003 ended, so the ad came right after the tutorials.

The numbers came from documents. The monetization design for our other game in the same repository, Arrow Knots, cited industry advice to hold the first interstitial back from the session start and picked a 90-second grace; Block Turn's PRD wrote the same 90 s and passed it to the shared ad pacing module. The session script first arrived with the launch prep on October 4. Before it, the repository has no record of anyone looking at the first few minutes on a time axis.

A test written with the agent had locked the behavior in. The device E2E suite committed that morning checked "banner shown from R004" as a pass condition in scenario S1. Under the PRD, R004 is the first real puzzle and should have no banner. The first draft of the launch plan raised the tutorial problem from a simulation only, and the cross-check disputed it. Once the device logs came in, the ad plan marked the issue as confirmed by measurement.

Run length decided which rule set the pace

In a 12-minute run of the three-move puzzle persona on the emulator, interstitials appeared at 181, 322, 465 and 611 s: gaps of 141 to 146 s, or 3.3 per 10 minutes. A puzzle takes about a minute, so "every 2 runs" was always met first, and the 120-second gap was what held the pace.

Classic went the other way. In a 14-minute S21 session, tutorials included, classic produced 2 runs (150 moves); the ad plan puts a run at about five minutes. The only interstitial was the one right after the tutorials. Counting the one rewarded revive the script accepted, the session still had just 1.4 full-screen ads per 10 minutes. Two classic runs take about ten minutes, so in classic the every-2-runs gate, not the 120 s gap, set the pace.

The launch plan's revenue simulator assumed a 90-second classic run, while the comment on that same line quoted the classic supply experiment's human target of 4 to 10 minutes. It also kept each interstitial on screen for 15 s; the session script closed them after 5 to 8 s, like a person. Replaying the puzzle persona in the simulator gave 4.09 interstitials in 12 minutes, matching the 4 measured, but a median gap of 162 s against the measured 141 to 146 s. Running it again on November 1 gave 4.09 and 162 s.

Tutorials excluded, classic counted twice, a 6-run gate dropped

A commit on the evening of October 4 carries the operator's three frequency decisions (the fourth item in that list is the banner slot rule below). Its message files them as "user decisions, from device measurements". The store listing's ad notice was changed in the same commit to say there is no banner and no between-run ad on the tutorials and the first three runs.

  • Tutorials no longer count toward the banner or the interstitial. In puzzle mode a new player sees neither before three real runs.
  • A classic game over counts as two runs toward the interstitial: the code adds two wins. So in classic the interstitial can come from the second game over for a new player, then after every game over, while the banner still waits for three runs. The 120 s gap and the session and daily caps stay, and the ad plan estimated that classic players would go from 1.4 to about 2 per 10 minutes.
  • No app open ad when the player returns in the middle of a run (a classic move made, or a puzzle piece placed and the puzzle not yet over).
fun onRunEnded(tutorial: Boolean = false, classic: Boolean = false) {
    if (tutorial) return
    runsEnded++
    prefs.edit().putInt(K_RUNS, runsEnded).apply()
    if (!enabled) return
    ads.onWin()
    if (classic) ads.onWin()
}

Raising the first-interstitial threshold from 3 runs to 6 would have been a one-constant change. The ad plan advised against it: once players who skip tutorials or abandon runs are in the mix, a raw count gives a grace of uneven length, so it recommended excluding tutorial solves instead. An interstitial after every run was ruled out because the 120 s gap already set the pace; only classic, with its long runs, moved to every game over. Removing the interstitial on the classic result screen's Home button was considered; the ad plan recommended keeping it, treating the break after a score screen as an allowed placement, and the code was left as is. The genre habit of an ad after every game over, as in Block Blast, was one input to the classic change.

When you set numbers meant to protect new players, leave tutorial levels out of the ad counters. Then check on a freshly installed device, from the log, at which second and after which run the first ad actually appears.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The banner slot rule changed five times, between an empty strip and a shifting layout

From October 3 to 5, each change fixed what the previous rule left behind, and the first one was made in the shared module before Block Turn existed.

Time (KST)Banner slot ruleWhat it left
Oct 3 16:38No space until ads may be requested (consent pending or refused)Empty strip on an offline device with consent already stored
Oct 4 02:05Zero height until the first ad actually arrivesA late fill pushed the board down (S21 classic, y 416 to 620)
Oct 4 17:14Slot reserved up frontOffline empty strip (listed as a drawback in the ad plan)
Oct 4 19:07Reserved only after a banner has filled in this processThe first fill in each process pushed the HUD down and put the banner where the home chip was
Oct 5 12:52Reserved from the first frame on every screen; collapses only on a failed loadOffline, an empty strip shows briefly, then folds

The last change lets the layout move only away from the ad: when the banner collapses, content moves up, and the ad never slides down onto the home and undo chips a finger is reaching for. The same commit stops reserving the slot and requesting ads after a failed load for 1, 2, 4 and up to 10 minutes, so the empty strip shows up less often.

Block Turn launched without Firebase, so D1 and D7 went unmeasured at launch

A device timeline shows when ads appear and how often, not whether players stay. Analytics arrived only on October 11, in version code 4, and there is still no remote config as of November 1. GA4 has tracked D1 since, but no one has compared it across the rule change yet. The ad plan gives PRD compliance and first impressions as the reasons for excluding tutorials, noting there is no number for how much retention would improve.

An app with remote config, analytics and enough players has a better basis: a 50/50 A/B test that changes frequency alone. Our PRD (§11.3) planned a 5% holdback of new players with no interstitials, but the ad plan dropped it because telling a 12% D7 from a 10% D7 at a 1:19 split would take about 42,000 installs; it plans a 50/50 single-variable A/B once there is scale. Without remote config, every frequency change in Block Turn needs an app update and a store review.

Each persona ran once, at a pace drawn from fixed ranges. That is not the spread of real player speeds, and the same rules already gave first ads at 91 s and 181 s. The builds used test ads, so fill rates may differ from live ads. The code shows an interstitial only when one is preloaded, so live counts can match these numbers or fall below them. What real players did in the first chapter is in Puzzle game day-one churn: the walls in chapter 1.

After pm clear, 12 to 15 minutes of logs, with S11 before S10

  1. Build with test ad IDs only. For a release build, keep minification on and keep only the ad and run-end log lines. Count the test and real IDs in the dex as in Why R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in a release AAB. Never drive a real-ID build with automated taps; those are invalid clicks.
  2. Have the app log one line each time it shows a full-screen ad (something like ads: show interstitial) and one line each time a run ends.
  3. Clear the app data for a fresh-install state, clear the log, and note the start time from the device clock.
  4. Play 12 to 15 minutes at human speed. Our session script spent 20 to 60 s thinking per puzzle, took 1.5 to 3.5 s per classic move, watched each interstitial for 5 to 8 s and accepted half of the revive offers. Run each mode separately.
  5. Read off the first full-screen ad, the gaps between interstitials, and the full-screen ads per 10 minutes (count / minutes x 10).
  6. Check the mid-run return rule by order. Make one move, go home, wait 250 s (longer than the 4-minute threshold) and come back: no app open ad (S11). Then make the same return from the home screen: one should appear (S10). Run S11 first: the day's app open cap (2 a day) is still unused then, which leaves the mid-run rule as the only reason no ad appeared.
  7. After changing a rule, rerun the same persona and compare.
adb shell pm clear <package>
adb logcat -c
adb shell date +%s.%N        # start time, device clock
adb logcat -v epoch -s ads:D GAME:D > session.log
# python timeline.py session.log <start time> <minutes played>
import re, sys
log, t0, minutes = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2]), float(sys.argv[3])
rx = re.compile(r"\s*([\d.]+)\s+\d+\s+\d+\s+\w\s+ads\s*:\s+show (\w+)")
shows = [(round(float(m[1]) - t0), m[2]) for m in map(rx.match, open(log, errors="ignore")) if m]
inter = [t for t, kind in shows if kind.lower() == "interstitial"]
print("first", shows[:1], "gaps", [b - a for a, b in zip(inter, inter[1:])],
      "per10min", round(len(shows) / (minutes / 10), 2))

The S21 and classic numbers after the change are still missing

As of November 1, the repository has no device re-measurement of the S21's first interstitial after tutorials stopped counting, and none of the classic rate after a game over started counting twice. The 314 s figure exists only in the commit message; its raw log was not kept in the repository, and neither the persona nor the build it used is recorded. The commit comment says there is no between-run ad in the first three runs, but in the code a classic-only player becomes eligible after the second game over. On November 1 the operator kept the code and decided to drop that sentence from the store notice. Checking the first interstitial by hand on a real-ID build is still listed for the operator in the launch rehearsal document.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Ads and metrics for two puzzle games: all 4 parts

  1. GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real: filtering out test phones and Play pre-launch and review devices
  2. App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings

Frequently asked questions

When should a puzzle game show its first interstitial?

In Block Turn's puzzle mode, with tutorials excluded, the first interstitial can come after three real runs once 90 s of the session have passed; in classic, where a game over counts twice, after the second game over. On the emulator on October 4, 2026, it came at 314 s, per the commit message.

Does the ad gap or "every N levels" decide how often interstitials show?

Run length decides. If two runs take longer than the 120 s gap, the every-2-runs gate sets the pace; otherwise the gap does. In the puzzle mode, where a run takes about a minute, the 120 s gap set the pace; in classic, where a run takes about five minutes, the every-2-runs gate did, so Block Turn now counts a classic game over twice.

How do I avoid an empty banner space when the device is offline?

Collapse the slot in the failed-load callback, then hold off on both the slot and the request for a while. Block Turn waits 1 minute, doubling up to 10 minutes. We dropped the zero-height-until-filled approach because a late fill pushed the board down.

Sources: the game repository's ad plan and launch rehearsal documents, PRD v2.1 §11.2, git history, the session script and the revenue simulator. Checked on 2026-11-01.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Every branch passed its AI review, and the merged code still had 12 defects

item.title: Claude Code subagent prompts after 5 cut-off runs – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

Claude Code subagent prompts: rules after 5 cut-off agents

Five of our subagents hit usage limits, and the reports they had created first were almost empty. The agents that took over started from the logs and edited files the first ones had left on disk.

Many agents, one repository 2/6

A Claude Code subagent that hits a session or weekly usage limit stops mid-task. Between September 7 and 10, 2026, five subagents preparing a Flutter peer-to-peer chat app for release stopped this way. Their brief (the written instructions each subagent gets) said to create the report first and fill it in as they worked, yet the cut-off reports were mostly empty sections. What made the handovers work was the files that piled up as a side effect of the work: logs, screenshots and edited files.

Five agents cut off, September 7 to 10

Three hit the session limit, one the weekly limit, and one has no recorded reason. In all five cases the agent that took over finished the job.

TaskWhy it stoppedReport when cut offAfter the handover
Emulator lab analysisNot recorded19 lines, every section "in progress"71 lines, 47 minutes later. Started from a device script and two screenshots
Docs mergeSession limit19-line skeleton; four edited docs left uncommitted192 lines. Done parts were not rewritten
Post-fix E2ESession limit41 lines, only the environment table338 lines in 50 minutes, reusing the raw logs
Device recheckWeekly limitEvidence nearly all collectedMain session judged it from 85 screenshots and 8 log types
String auditSession limit8-line skeleton, no files left1,046 lines, measured again from scratch

A 33-line shared brief: six bans and a report format

The brief had a one-line goal, verified facts about the environment, six hard rules and a report format; each agent got its topic separately. The environment facts listed the Flutter version, two emulators, and "no physical device, no macOS." The rules, in short:

  1. Do not install system packages or add dependencies. If one is needed, write "approval needed" in the report.
  2. Do not upload anything. Outputs stay as files in the repository.
  3. In the analysis phase, do not touch app code. Write scripts and docs only.
  4. No blanket search-and-replace. Move files to a temp folder instead of rm -rf.
  5. Cite outside policies with a URL and a check date; label guesses as guesses.
  6. Create the report early at a fixed path and update it as you go, "so partial results survive if the session ends."

The findings table had six columns: ID, severity (Blocker/High/Medium/Low), description, evidence (file and line or URL), proposed fix, and how to verify. All 17 reports kept that format; the 16 with content held 233 findings, 15 of them Blockers, and the fix stage took its work by those IDs.

The bans were used. Thirteen analysis reports say "approval needed," and a proposal to add an icon-generation package became a script using a Python imaging library that was already installed. Keeping the ban list in one file that every run reads is the same idea as our permission table for a scheduled AI agent. The allowed severity values did not hold, though: reports invented "Info" and "Low to Medium."

Why the early reports were empty

Rule 6 asked agents to create and update the report but never said when to update it. Judging by the records, the verdicts lived only in each agent's conversation, not in a file, and no agent tidied its report before it was cut off.

The post-fix E2E report came closest to the rule. Its header said "if the session ends, treat empty cells as not measured," yet its results table was completely empty. The same folder held two logcats (about 100,000 and 90,000 lines), a server log, 43 screenshots and raw round-trip timings for 11 messages. The calculation script used the wrong log anchor, matched only one of them, and reported n=1, 11 ms.

The agents taking over read git diff and the raw folder first

The docs-merge agent stopped with its edits still in the working tree. Only the main session was allowed to commit, so it committed that state as partial work. The next agent began with git diff to see what had already changed: every item in the agent instruction file and 7 of 8 in the security doc were done, and the other nine docs were untouched. It finished 19 files without rewriting the done parts.

The agent that took over post-fix E2E kept the raw output for build, install, connection and message sending, and ran only the remaining tests. It did not re-measure latency either: it fixed the log anchor and recomputed the ten messages already sent, getting p50 61 ms and p95 74 ms.

The string audit was reading code and judging it, so it left no files. The next agent re-parsed 2,864 string literals in 93 files from scratch and judged the 464 that can reach the screen. What happened to the contrast checker the same day is in our contrast checker skipped 40% of the text.

In a subagent brief, say where and when to write raw evidence before you say "create the report first."

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The "how to verify" column corrected a prediction

The security analysis read the code and predicted that an app restored from Android auto-backup would lose its encryption key and become permanently unusable. A lab agent followed that row's "how to verify" cell, running backup, uninstall, reinstall and restore for real, and the app did not lock up. After a key error it went back to setup and created a new profile; the old key and chat history quietly disappeared. The conclusion changed, but the proposed fix (turn off backup) was still needed.

Instructions were wrong at times too. The UI-fix agent reported that 3 of the 8 proposed patches from analysis were wrong or incomplete and fixed them before applying. The post-fix E2E instructions mapped ports in the wrong direction, so the app would have connected to itself; the agent reversed the mapping and noted it in the environment table.

What if subagents committed their own work?

Letting subagents commit would protect against cut-offs. This round forbade it: several agents edited files in the same working tree at once, and a single git stash or git checkout could wipe out someone else's changes. The price was uncommitted work after each cut-off, which the main session committed instead. How sessions collided in one working tree is in Multiple Claude Code sessions: one owner per file.

Nobody wrote a separate brief per agent either. The three later briefs (fixes, review fixes, full audit) said to "apply the shared brief as is" and added only what changed at that stage: edit only files you own, do not commit, write tests that fail when the guard is removed.

Read-only work leaves nothing behind

Taking over from files on disk only worked for tasks that create files as they go. Work that only reads code and judges it, like the string audit or a code review, leaves nothing. The environment section differs per machine, so reuse the template but check that section on your own setup. Whether these rules reduced defects cannot be said; there was no round to compare against.

A brief template and the commands for a handover

This template merges the rules of the shared brief and the fix-stage brief, and adds a path for raw output and a unit of update.

# <round> shared brief (<date>)
Goal: <one line>
## Environment (verified only)
- Tool paths and versions: <...>
- Devices available: <...> / not available: <...>
## Do not
1. Install or add packages. If one is needed, write "approval needed"
2. Upload anything. Outputs are files in the repository only
3. Edit files you do not own. Put requests in "requests to other owners"
4. commit, stash or checkout (the main session commits)
5. Guess without saying so. Outside docs get a URL and a check date
## Output paths
- Report: <dir>/<NN>_<topic>.md
  Create it first; the first line is exactly "Status: in progress"
- Raw: <dir>/raw/<NN>_*
  Save command output, logs and screenshots as soon as you get them
- Add a table row each time one finding or one measurement is done
## Report format
Summary / What was checked / Findings / Remaining unknowns
| ID | Severity | Description | Evidence (file:line / URL) | Proposed fix | How to verify |
Severity is exactly one of Blocker, High, Medium, Low

When taking over, read git and the raw folder before the report.

  1. Find unfinished reports by the status line or by the placeholder line that opens an empty section.
    git grep -lE "^(Status: in progress|\(in progress\))" <commit> -- <report dirs>
  2. See what the previous session changed.
    git diff --stat <start commit>..<partial commit> -- <owned files>
  3. List the raw folder. If a measurement has a suspiciously small n, check the calculation script before measuring again.
  4. Set the report's status to done and add one line on who took over what.

One line per verdict is still untested

For work with no side files, like the string audit, the next round will count how many lines survive a cut-off when the agent writes one line per verdict.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Many agents, one repository: all 6 parts

  1. Claude Code parallel agents: 10 workstreams, 3 at a time
  2. Multiple Claude Code sessions in one repo: a file owner table

FAQ

When a subagent hits its session limit, is its work kept?

Only what it wrote to disk. The five cut-off reports were mostly empty sections; the handovers started from logs, screenshots and edited files produced along the way.

What should go first in a subagent prompt?

What not to do, where outputs and raw evidence go, and the report format. This round's shared brief covered those plus environment facts in 33 lines; each agent got its topic separately.

Does letting subagents commit solve the cut-off problem?

This round did not try it. Several agents shared one working tree, so only the main session committed; it committed cut-off work as partial and said in the message what was left.

Sources: the chat app repository's git history, the shared brief and three later briefs, 17 analysis reports and the fix reports. Times are Korea time; report lengths were recounted from git on November 13, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check

item.title: HWP compatibility test: Save As in Hancom Docs – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

Seven HWP files edited by our app all opened in Hancom Office Viewer with no damage notice. Save As in Hancom Docs needed a human sign-in first; both files tried afterwards re-saved.

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer 7/8

To check that HWP files your app edits still open and re-save in Hancom's own apps, open the original and the result through the same screens and compare them. The re-save step sits behind a Hancom Docs sign-in, though, so an AI agent cannot finish the check alone. On October 18, 2026, on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15), we opened seven HWP files edited with the code of our app HWP Viewer SugarDoc in the two Android apps from Hancom, the company behind the HWP format and the Hangul word processor. All seven opened with no damage notice and their unedited pages matched the originals; only an emoji drew as a blank. Re-saving was tried on two of them, h3 and h7, after the operator signed in, and both passed (171,008 B and 171,520 B).

Four pass criteria, and the agent could reach three

Before edit was switched on, the plan held a Hancom compatibility table. Each document gets the body and table-cell edits that apply to it, plus one file with the special characters < & > " ' and an emoji, and one long insertion that pushes text onto a new page. A file passes four checks: (1) it opens with no damage or repair notice, (2) the edited text is visible, (3) unedited pages match the original, (4) Hancom can save it again. Form-field filling had already been cut from the edit scope, for the reasons in We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug, so the form-field column was dropped too.

The table started out as a job for a person. On October 18 the operator handed it to the agent, to run on the S21, and limited it to installing free apps: no payments, no sign-ins. The plan that the agent could finish the table alone broke on check 4. The agent installed Hancom Office Viewer (com.tf.thinkdroid.viewer) and Hancom Docs (com.hancom.docs.suite 2.0.15.544) from Play. Viewer had no save function. Hancom Docs could save, and its first screen asked for a sign-in. At 17:24 the agent took a screenshot of the sign-in screen and backed out.

The test files came from node, running the app's own edit code

The table calls for Korean text and an emoji. adb shell input text, the usual way to type into an app from a script, only takes ASCII, so driving SugarDoc's screen could not produce those files. The agent ran the edit code the app runs inside its WebView (pick a target, apply, export and reopen) in node, on the same pinned rhwp 0.8.6 engine (measured in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents). Each result then went through the app's Kotlin preview scrub and save gate; all seven passed. The on-device save path was covered separately that day by a device E2E run that typed ASCII markers.

The generator the agent wrote only picked text runs of two or more characters, and the form document had nothing but empty paragraphs and a form field, so h5 came back with no target (BODY:NONE). It has the same cause as the empty-paragraph case in the save gate note. The agent switched h5 to typing into an empty paragraph, rebuilt the set a minute later, and put the seven files and their originals into the S21's Download folder.

Eight screenshots per file, and h7 checked by eye

Sending an HWP to Viewer through a VIEW intent made Viewer ask for "All files access". The agent tapped "Later" and found another way in: Viewer's own Open button, which hands off to the system file picker and needs no such permission.

The comparison script opens the original and the edited file the same way, takes eight screenshots at the same scroll steps, and counts pixels whose grayscale difference is above 40. It also searches the screen's view tree for Korean words meaning damaged, repair, error, cannot open and not supported. The first two runs opened nothing, because the picker started in another folder; a step that walks into the folder fixed that. The same swipe does not stop at exactly the same place twice (4 to 16 px apart on files whose pages did not move), so the script slides the edited shot up or down by at most 70 px (staying clear of the status and tool bars) to the best match before counting. Screens with a nonzero count were turned into side-by-side images and reviewed.

FileEditPagesScreens with 0 diffWhere it differed
h1marker text after a body text run3→36/8the edited line and the next one reflowed
h2table cell text3→37/8that cell (1,164 px)
h3body and table cell1→10/8the two edits (4,037 px on each screen)
h4cell and body, document with a form field3→36/8the edits; the form field placeholder unchanged
h5text in an empty paragraph of a form1→10/8the new line (784 px); form objects unchanged
h6special characters and an emoji (U+1F600)3→36/8the edited line; characters shown, emoji blank
h7a sentence of about 480 characters1→20/8everything moved down a page

h3 and h5 are one page long, so all eight screenshots show the same view and catch the same edit each time. No file produced a warning. Viewer also raised nothing about the preview streams, which the app replaces on save (PrvText with spaces, PrvImage with a blank image).

The emoji is still U+1F600 when rhwp reopens the file, yet Viewer drew it as a blank. We had no emoji document authored in Hancom's own software to compare with, so we do not know whether the font or the file is responsible. SugarDoc's edit sheet does not block emoji input.

The release conditions disagreed, and the re-save came after release

At 20:07 the 1.3.0 commit that turned edit on carried the first version of the QA document: open and display 7 of 7, re-save not checked. It asked the operator to try "Save As" on at least one result file (h3 and h7 suggested) on a signed-in device before release, and to switch edit off (flagEdit=false) if that failed. The agent left edit on because no file had failed; the coordinating agent session that received its report advised against production until the check was done. The operator approved the production release, and at 20:33 a commit recorded it with "Hancom re-save unverified". The release conditions also differed between documents: the plan listed all four checks and the production ban, while the decision table in the design document only blocked release if check 1 failed.

The agent does not type passwords or create accounts, so it asked the operator to sign in; at 20:57 the operator said the S21 was signed in to Hancom Docs. Hancom Docs then asked for "All files access", and the agent would not switch on a security permission itself. Its first directions pointed to the permission list on the app info screen, and the operator replied that the permission was not there. On this S21 it sat under special access in Settings. The agent opened that settings screen directly with an intent, and the operator switched it on at 21:01.

The first attempt to open the Hancom Docs editor showed Google Play's "app not recognized" screen (the app had been installed from Play). To see whether our file was the cause, the agent opened the unedited original of h3 the same way, through the file manager's "open with". The original opened in the editor, and the Play screen never came back. The record attributes it to a one-off check on Hancom's side; nobody confirmed the cause.

At 21:05 the edited h3 opened in the editor with no damage notice and both edits visible. "Save As" from the menu wrote resave_h3.hwp (171,008 B), which reopened with the same text and layout. h7 opened still pushed from one page to two; resave_h7.hwp (171,520 B) reopened with the two-page layout, table and logo unchanged. A commit recorded both at 21:10.

Do not call a file compatible because it opens. The bar is a re-save in the vendor's app, and if that step sits behind a sign-in, name the person who does that step in the table before the work starts.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Direct editor launch, pixel judging for h7, desktop Hangul: not used

Launching the Hancom Docs editor activity straight from adb would have skipped the file manager, but it was refused with not exported, so the agent went back to the file manager's "open with". In h7 everything moved down, and all eight screens still differed after alignment (168,496 to 221,626 px each), so we dropped the pixel count for that file and judged it from side-by-side images: the table and logo were intact and the text ran onto page 2. Checking in the desktop Hangul word processor was out from the start, because we had no copy to use.

The pixel diff only aligns vertically, and the re-saved files were only reopened

The comparison only aligns vertically. A different zoom level or horizontal offset is not corrected either, so those screens, like the page-shifted h7, need a person comparing them side by side.

Both re-saved files came out smaller than ours (both 235,520 B, from originals of 292,352 B). We never compared their records, so we do not know what went; reopening and reading the text and layout was the whole check. No Korean edit made through SugarDoc's WebView on a phone has been opened in Hancom's apps. Later on the same evening, after the test files were built, the released edit code stopped offering empty paragraphs without controls as edit targets. The paragraph h5 typed into holds one control (engine query), so that rule does not apply to it. One device (the S21, Android 15) and one Hancom Docs version (2.0.15.544) were used.

Running the same round trip for your own format

  1. Write the table first: one file per kind of edit (body, table cell, special characters, emoji, a long insertion that moves text to the next page, a form document), four checks each. Put a person's name in every cell that needs a sign-in or a special access permission.
  2. Build test files through the same code path as the app, and keep only those that pass the app's save gate. Put each original next to them with an orig_ prefix.
  3. If the vendor app (made by the company behind the format, here Hancom) asks for broad permissions, look for its own Open menu and the system file picker first.
  4. Open original and result the same way, screenshot the same scroll steps, align vertically, count differing pixels. Look by eye at every nonzero screen and at any file whose pages moved.
  5. Search the view tree for warnings such as damage or repair notices.
  6. In the app that can save, use "Save As" to a new name, reopen it, check text and layout, and note the size.
  7. Mark anything you could not run as unchecked, and make sure every document that sets release conditions uses the same checks.
# apps that handle the format; the all-files access settings screen
adb shell cmd package query-activities --brief -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -t application/x-hwp -d content://media/external/downloads/1
adb shell am start -a android.settings.MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION \
  -d package:com.hancom.docs.suite
# differing pixels after vertical alignment (margins for a 1080x2400 S21,
# shortened from the session script)
from PIL import Image, ImageChops
def diff(a_png, b_png, top=300, bottom=330):
    A, B = Image.open(a_png).convert("L"), Image.open(b_png).convert("L")
    bot = A.height - bottom
    def count(dy, k=1):
        a = A.crop((0, top, A.width, bot))
        b = B.crop((0, top + dy, B.width, bot + dy))
        if k > 1:
            a = a.resize((a.width // k, a.height // k))
            b = b.resize((b.width // k, b.height // k))
        d = ImageChops.difference(a, b).point(lambda v: 1 if v > 40 else 0)
        return sum(d.getdata())
    ok = [d for d in range(-120, 121, 2)
          if top + d >= 230 and bot + d <= A.height - 260]
    dy = min(ok, key=lambda d: count(d, 4))
    return count(dy), dy

On the S21 the first command listed Hancom Docs and Viewer among the apps that open HWP.

Five files and the desktop word processor are still unchecked

h1, h2, h4, h5 and h6 have not been re-saved in Hancom Docs, and the repository shows no change through its October 29 commits. That set includes the emoji file h6 and h4, the document with a form field. Opening and saving in the desktop Hangul word processor, and the cause of the blank emoji, are also still open.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer: all 8 parts

  1. We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug
  2. A malicious file set for a document viewer: ZIP bombs, CFB loops and XSS, generated and wired into tests

FAQ

Can Hancom Office Viewer save an HWP file under a new name?

Not the version we used on the S21 on October 18, 2026: it had no save function. We used "Save As" in the Hancom Docs editor after signing in.

Where is "All files access" for Hancom Docs on Android?

On our S21 (Android 15) it was not in the app's permission list but under special access in Settings. Over adb, am start -a android.settings.MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION -d package:com.hancom.docs.suite opens that screen directly.

Sources: the SugarDoc repository's Hancom compatibility QA document, 1.3.0 release record, plan and design documents, git history and that evening's work session log (as of October 31).

Hancom and HWP are trademarks of Hancom Inc. This note is not affiliated with or endorsed by Hancom Inc.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates

item.title: Parallel AI agent branches: 12 integration defects – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Every branch passed its AI review, and the merged code still had 12 defects

A branch review reads only its own diff. After merging parallel branches, run a separate review that reads only the merged code; ours confirmed 12 defects that per-branch review and CI had missed.

Many agents, one repository 5/6

Hand each feature to its own AI coding agent on its own branch, and every branch can pass review and tests while the places where they meet still disagree. In the early hours of October 10, 2026, after the 13 branches of AXFamily, a family calendar app we are building, were merged, review agents that read only the merged code confirmed 12 defects. Neither the existing tests nor git conflicts had shown any of them, and 10 turned out to be broken agreements between code written by two different packages.

From the 01:51 merges to the 05:34 PR merge

The first parallel wave ran one workflow that put every package through the same steps: one agent implemented it, three agents reviewed the branch through security, cost and correctness lenses, and a fix agent addressed their findings and got the PR to green CI. How the 13 branches were merged is in Multiple Claude Code sessions: one owner per file.

Time (KST)What happened
01:51All 13 branches merged into the integration branch in just over two minutes
02:09Minimal fixes for 6 package pairs the merge broke
02:53 to 04:23Three wiring commits applying cross-package decisions: contract, then server, then app
04:29Six review agents start reading the merged code; done in 6 to 9 minutes
04:38Each of 12 blockers and majors goes to its own refuting agent; all 12 confirmed within a minute
05:28Fix commit: 115 files, 2,088 lines added
05:3411 CI jobs pass; integration PR merged

The first assumption: green tests meant the integration was done

The plan described the wave as "parallel feature work (separate files only)", and its conflict rules were written per shared file. The integration step was told to resolve conflicts keeping both sides' intent, run every suite, and fix integration breakage minimally.

The integration agent finished by that standard. Its PR reported five suites, 2,115 tests in all (977 of them Flutter tests, 5 Rules tests skipped), all passing. None of the 12 defects found later changed any of those numbers. They surfaced only in the review step that had been placed at the end of the workflow in advance.

32 findings from six lenses; 12 survived refutation

The six lenses were Firestore security rules (Rules) and contract, function security, cost, app security and privacy, app UX, and flow tracing, which followed the core flow in code from sign-in to account deletion. Of 32 findings, 20 were minor and 12 blocker or major. Two of the 12 were the same defect found from two sides, so there were 11 distinct defects.

The refutation prompt told each agent to read the code and try to break the finding, and to reject it unless the defect could be shown. Each refuter returned a verdict in 16 to 25 seconds, citing files and line numbers. On the missing index, the verdict even pointed out that other collections queried the same way already had their composite indexes.

10 of the 12 sat between two packages

Rewriting each confirmed defect as "which two pieces of code believed different things" gives the table below. The classification is ours, made while writing this note; app feature details are kept short.

Lens (severity)The two sidesThe mismatch
Rules and contract, function security (major, same defect twice)Rules vs. a function added during wiringRules let any adult in the household edit a field the function trusted as proof of consent eligibility
Rules and contract (major)Records screen query vs. index fileNo composite index for a sorted query
Function security (major)Revocation check vs. ownership transferRevocation re-evaluated against the revoker's current role, so a role change undid it
App security and privacy (major)Records cleanup vs. sign-out cleanup listCleanup never registered, so a failure was never retried
App security and privacy (major)Inside the share inboxCopied files left behind when the queue overflowed or got corrupted
App UX (blocker)Billing entry widget vs. family screenZero callers of the widget
App UX (major)Household deletion function vs. settings screenThe app never sent the cancel flag and read the cancelled reply as an error
App UX (major)UI spec vs. bottom action buttonButton on tabs the spec excluded, with the wrong label
App UX (major)Banner slot vs. screen state reportsOne failure blocked banners for the whole session (spec says per screen)
Flow tracing (blocker)App capture vs. AI extraction functionFor PDF sources the app sent image/webp; the server accepted only application/pdf
Flow tracing (major)Household picker vs. calendar screens and billingThe picker wrote a new key, the screens read an old key nothing wrote, billing used the first household

Only two stayed inside one package: the share inbox files and the bottom button. In the other 10, each side was correct on its own. In the PDF case, the app sent a first-page thumbnail exactly as its own code comment said, and the server counted pages from PDF bytes exactly as the contract said at the time.

Each branch review read only its own diff

The branch review prompt had each reviewer read git diff origin/develop...origin/<branch>. The index file was already on the development branch and the Rules package was changing it separately, but it never appeared in the diff of the agent reviewing the sorted query. The server check that accepts only PDFs was likewise outside the app capture reviewer's diff.

The billing package's review had already found one of these. Told to grep for production callers of every new API, it found that nothing called the billing entry widget, but rated it minor; a re-review just before integration raised it to major. The call belonged in the family screen file, which the file owner rules kept the billing side from touching, so the item went into the PR's "to align with other packages" section. The integration workflow's wiring list, though, had been fixed in its script before that re-review, and the item came back as a blocker in the integration review.

Tests ran per package against that package's own fakes and the Firestore emulator, which does not enforce composite indexes. The contract's query table listed a collection that the same document's required-index list left out. CI passed, and only production would have answered with FAILED_PRECONDITION. (It was caught before any production deploy.)

Agent-written comments and tests also hid mismatches. A comment in the calendar code said the active-household key was "written by the household switcher", but git grep found no code that wrote it. The bottom button test was named "on every tab", locking in a placement the spec had ruled out.

After merging parallel branches, run a review that reads only the merged code, however many branch reviews came before.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The check we kept: a sorted-query-to-index table

The fix commit added, for each defect, a test that fails on the old code; for the Rules, index and consent fixes the fix was actually reverted to watch the test fail (the technique is in Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting guards). Two fixes became checks for the next mismatch of the same kind.

For indexes, the Rules test suite gained a table of app queries that use orderBy. Each row names the app file, the query and the index it needs, and the test looks for that index in the index file. A final test compares how often orderBy: ' appears in app code, and in which files, with the table, so anyone adding a sorted query has to add a row first.

const count = (rel) => (readFileSync(resolve(appRoot, rel), 'utf8').match(/orderBy:\s*'/g) ?? []).length;
// …
expect(actual).toEqual(expected);
// fail if a file outside the table uses orderBy: '<field>'
const all = execSync(`grep -rlE "^\\s*orderBy: '" lib || true`, { cwd: appRoot, encoding: 'utf8' })
  .split('\n').filter(Boolean).map((f) => f.trim());
expect(all.sort()).toEqual(files.sort());

By October 13, three more app files with sorted queries had been added to the table. For household selection, the app session's current household became the single source of truth; with two or more households and no valid selection, the picker returns null instead of falling back to the first one.

Other routes: a staging project, shared test vectors

A real Firestore project would have exposed the missing index at once. The plan had postponed a staging project until after launch ("low benefit for the risk, one more place that can charge us"), and the device runs that morning used an emulator backend to keep costs at zero.

One method had already worked. The billing tests were written to read a shared vector file (expected answers for whether a subscription counts as active) that the billing server package would add, and skipped while it was missing. Right after the merge they ran and caught the app and server disagreeing on entitlement. Contracts without a vector file, like consent eligibility or household selection, were out of its reach.

What a read-only review missed

Three rounds of device E2E the same day found more runtime defects. One was a Firestore trigger that crashed without a default Admin app, and the fix report itself says the Android side got unit tests only. Why device checks run separately even after a review converges on zero is in AI code review: fix only what survives refutation.

Each finding got one refuter for 16 to 25 seconds, so 12 out of 12 surviving is not evidence that refutation can be dropped. And the app UX lens compared screens against a written UI spec; without one, that lens has nothing to compare against.

How to run integration review as its own step

  1. Collect every branch PR's "to align with other packages" list into the integration task list, and finalize the wiring list only after every branch review is done.
  2. Once everything is merged and green, hand the integration diff to one read-only agent per area. Ask for concrete defects with evidence only, each one challenged by the reviewer before it is reported.
    git diff --stat origin/develop...origin/<integration-branch>
  3. Count production callers for every new widget, function and parameter, excluding the file that defines it. Zero is a finding by itself.
    git grep -n "<NewWidget>(" -- <app source dir> ':!<defining file>'
  4. Send each blocker and major to a different agent to refute, and drop anything that cannot be shown.
  5. For each confirmed defect, add a test that fails on the old code, and revert the fix once to watch it fail.
  6. Turn each defect type into a check: a table check when both sides can be counted, like queries and indexes; a shared vector file read by both sides' tests when it is a decision rule.

Next to check: server queries and gaps in the table

The sorted-query table counts only the orderBy: ' string in app code. Server function queries were still added to the required index list by hand on October 13. Whether server queries can be counted the same way is the next thing to try.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Many agents, one repository: all 6 parts

  1. Keeping a static site safe when several AI agents edit it: one --check before every commit
  2. AI code review findings: fix only what survives refutation

FAQ

If every branch had an AI review, do I still need an integration review?

Yes. Every branch here was reviewed by three agents, and the merged code still had 12 blocker or major defects. A branch review reads only its own diff, so it misses the other side of a contract whenever that side is not in the diff.

Will Firestore emulator tests catch a missing composite index?

No. The emulator does not enforce composite indexes, so tests pass with the index missing. Add a static check that matches the app's sorted queries against the index file, or run the queries against a real project.

How long did the integration review take?

Review took 6 to 9 minutes and refutation under a minute; the fix took about 49 minutes to its commit and about 55 minutes to the PR merge. From the 01:51 merges to the 05:34 PR merge was 3 hours 43 minutes.

Sources: the app repository's git history, the integration and billing PR descriptions, the fix report, and the integration workflow script and run log (rechecked October 31, 2026). Times are KST.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.description:
AXFamily

Your family's week, and who's on each one AXFamily is a shared family calendar for Android that gathers your family's events and to-dos in one place.

Google Play AXFamily: Family Calendar

Get it on Google Play AXFamily privacy policy

Use it to

  • Stop sorting out school and class schedules over chat every time
  • Share childcare with grandparents and decide who takes care of what
  • Keep track of everything when you're raising kids on your own
  • Get family plans out of the group chat and into one place
  • Plan a trip with kids around nap and meal times

What it does

  • Decide who does what

    Tap "I'll do it" on a to-do so your family sees who's on it, or "Can't do it" when you can't this time. Check off things to bring one by one, and turn on notifications for reminders before events.

  • A heads-up every Sunday evening

    With notifications on, every Sunday evening you see the week ahead: to-dos nobody took, clashing events, deadlines and birthdays within 7 days. The list is free and doesn't count toward AI uses.

  • An AI assistant that answers from your records

    In "Ask the family", ask "What am I in charge of this week?" It answers from your family's events and to-dos and shows which record it used. If nothing matches, it says so. Say "Add groceries Saturday at 10" and it drafts the event; it's saved only when you check it and tap Save.

  • School notices in one place

    Upload a photo of a school notice, and AI finds its dates and things to bring. It's added to your calendar only after you check it and tap Save.

  • Trip and weekend helper

    Pick where, when and who's going for a day-by-day plan draft, with packing, a budget and who does what. Add your kids' nap and meal times and the plan fits around them. Items marked "Forgot" last trip are flagged for the next one. Opening hours, prices and travel times are marked "Check details", and the plan is added only after every adult on the trip says yes.

  • Family memories

    Within a week after a trip or event, it suggests an album of its events and photos. Ask "When was our beach trip last year?" to find it. Only records of adults who agreed to AI are used.

  • Private by default

    Even on a shared family calendar, new events and records start private. Share them with the whole family or chosen people, or pick "Time only" to show when you're busy, not what it is. No one else, not even the family admin, sees your private items, including through the AI.

At a glance

FamilySend your partner or the kids' grandparents an invite message and they join the same family. Kids are added as profiles, no sign-in or phone needed.
AccountGoogle account or email, age 19 or older
PlansEvents, to-dos, reminders, the Sunday heads-up and sharing settings are free (5 AI uses a month, 1,000 photos, one banner ad). Family Plus subscription: no ads for the family, 150 AI uses a month, 10,000 photos, a three-line AI summary on Sundays, person card suggestions
AIGoogle's Gemini model. Each adult turns it on with their own consent; events, to-dos and reminders all work without AI.
AI usesA question, a notice photo or a PDF page uses 1. A weekend plan uses 2, a 1 to 3 day trip 3, and 4 to 5 days 4. Uses are shared by the family and refill on the 1st of each month.
InternetNeeded (records are shared with your family).
LanguagesKorean and English
Android12L or later
Package namecom.sugarmount.axfamily
Developersimpest (SugarMount)

Data and permissions

  • Family records are never shared with advertisers. Personalized ads are shown only if you agree.
  • Photos are uploaded as small copies without location data. Originals stay on your phone.
  • For children under 14, names and notes aren't sent to the AI. Events and trips a child joins use an age group (like "elementary") instead of a name. Titles and destinations are still sent.
  • A child's notice photo is read by AI only with a guardian's consent.
  • Health records are not sent to the AI unless you turn them on, and then only your own.
  • Delete your account and records in the app's Settings or from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions separately in Google Play.

See AXFamily privacy policy for details.

What it can't do

  • AI can be wrong. AI text is labeled "AI-generated", and you can report odd answers right in the app. Always check opening hours, prices and travel times yourself.
  • AI never changes your events or to-dos by itself. Nothing is saved until you check it.
  • AI has daily limits (20 per person, 30 per family). If AI fails to answer, uses are given back (up to 4 a month).
  • AXFamily isn't made by a school. Upload the notices you receive yourself.

Do kids need an account?

No. Kids are added as profiles without signing in, and they don't need a phone. Accounts are for adults aged 19 or older.

Can I use it without AI?

Yes. Events, to-dos and reminders all work without AI. AI turns on only for adults who each agree to it.

Does the Sunday heads-up use AI uses?

No. The Sunday evening heads-up is free and doesn't count toward AI uses. Album suggestions don't use them either.

Can my partner see my private events?

No. Items you keep private can't be seen by anyone else, even the family admin, and don't show up when someone else asks the AI.

How do I delete my account?

Delete it in the app's Settings or request it from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions separately in Google Play.
