item.title: TrimBox: 3D trunk packing for camping gear – SugarMount
item.description:
TrimBox

TrimBox is an Android app that packs your camping gear into the 3D trunk of one of 10 mini cars, SUVs and minivans and shows whether it all fits and the tailgate closes.

Google Play TrimBox: Car Trunk Packing 3D

Get it on Google PlayTrimBox privacy policy

Use it to

  • Find out before a camping trip whether everything fits in one go
  • Decide what to load first: tent, cooler, chairs or table
  • Check whether new gear fits alongside what you already pack, before buying it
  • Compare your current car and your next one with the same gear

What it does

  • 10 mini cars, SUVs and minivans

    Kia Sorento (MQ4) 5-seat and 7-seat with the 3rd row folded, Hyundai Santa Fe (MX5) 5-seat and 7-seat with the 3rd row folded, Hyundai Palisade (LX3) 7-seat with the 3rd row folded, Kia Carnival (KA4) with the 3rd row up or the rear rows stowed (7-seat or 9-seat), Kia Sportage (NQ5), Tesla Model Y (2025+), Hyundai IONIQ 5 (2024+), and the mini cars Kia Ray, Hyundai Casper and Casper Electric with the 2nd row up or folded. Each one has its own trunk size, wheel arches, sloped tailgate, seatback angle and rear view. The Sorento is checked against published tape measurements; the other nine are estimated from specs and official cargo volumes, and the vehicle menu marks each one Measured or Estimated.

  • One tap: Will it fit?

    Tells you whether the current layout fits as it is, and if not, how many items are blocked and why: wheel arch, ceiling, tailgate, seatback or another item. It shows how many a repack would fit and applies that layout with one tap.

  • See if the tailgate closes

    If the top of a load hits the sloped tailgate, it turns red and shows how many centimeters stick out. If not everything fits, it suggests how far to slide the 2nd row forward (Sorento, IONIQ 5, Carnival 7-seat, Ray, Casper, Casper Electric).

  • Just pick. It packs itself.

    Gear goes into the trunk as you add it: big items low and deep, long items lying down, small items in the gaps, with the wheel arches used as shelves. Items of 20 kg or more stay on the floor, things you reach for often, like a cooler or first-aid kit, go near the tailgate, and soft bags are squeezed only as much as needed. It never returns a layout with floating or overlapping items.

  • Loading order, step by step

    Every item gets a number in the order to load it, and you can step through them one at a time. Tips point out heavy items on top of light ones and everyday items buried deep inside.

  • 197 camping items

    Packed sizes of tents, tarps, tables, chairs, coolers, sleeping bags, mats, stoves, storage boxes and car camping gear, plus 8 suitcases and 5 moving boxes. Search and set a quantity, or add a whole set: Minimal for 2, Family of 4 or Solo backpacking. Enter the size of anything that is missing.

  • Same gear, another car

    Switch vehicles and your gear stays. Repack and tap Will it fit? to compare your current car and your next one with the same load.

  • Save & share card

    One card with the layout and the numbered loading order, saved to your gallery or shared with your family. It takes one short ad per layout; if no ad loads, the card is made anyway.

  • Move things yourself, and save

    Rotate and zoom the 3D trunk, drag items, rotate or delete them, undo and redo. Start over clears the gear and keeps the vehicle. Your work saves automatically. Named saves start with 1 slot and gain one more for each short ad you watch (up to 5), and opening a save never needs an ad. You can also export a layout as a file and import it again.

  • Pro (one-time purchase)

    With Pro, ads stop showing everywhere in the app and named saves are unlimited. It is a one-time purchase, not a subscription; after reinstalling or on a new device, tap Restore purchase in About with the same Google account. Vehicles, the check, auto-pack and the loading guide all work without Pro.

At a glance

StatusGoogle Play
Supported vehicles10 mini cars, SUVs and minivans in 17 setups, plus Custom (a box from sizes you enter). Kia Sorento MQ4 tape-measured; the other nine estimated from specs
PriceFree to install, with ads. Pro is a one-time purchase (not a subscription); Google Play shows the price in your currency
StorageLayouts stay on your phone. We run no servers.
InternetNot needed for the check, auto-pack or saving. Only ads, usage analytics and the Pro purchase use it.
AdsGoogle AdMob: an app open ad now and then when you return after a while (max 2 a day), rewarded ads you choose for a card or a save slot, and a banner at the bottom of My layouts. Nothing is shown while checking, packing or following the loading steps
LanguagesKorean and English (follows your phone's language by default; change it from the app menu)
AccountNot needed.
Package namecom.sugarmount.trimbox
Developersimpest (SugarMount)

Data and permissions

  • The app shows Google AdMob ads. The ads SDK shares the advertising ID and app set ID, approximate location estimated from the IP address, app interactions and diagnostics with Google for advertising, analytics and fraud prevention.
  • In the EEA, the UK and Switzerland an ad consent screen (Google UMP) appears, and you can change your choice any time in Privacy options in About. You can reset or delete your advertising ID in Android Settings.
  • Google Play handles the Pro purchase. The app never receives card numbers or other payment details; it turns Pro on from the purchase state Google Play reports and keeps only a Pro yes/no flag on your phone. Once you have Pro, the ads SDK is not started when you open the app.
  • Only the ads SDK, Google Play billing and, from version 1.0.1, usage analytics (Google Analytics for Firebase) use the internet. Analytics sends fixed usage events such as checks and auto-packs as counts only, never the advertising ID, layout names, gear names or dimensions. There is no account or sign-in, and no crash reporting SDK.
  • Layouts, their names and the number of save slots you have unlocked are stored only on your phone and are never put into ad requests.
  • Save & share card, layout file export and import, and feedback email happen only when you tap them, through Android's share sheet, photo storage, file picker or your mail app. The Google Play link in the shared text carries only a tag that marks the visit as coming from a share (utm_source=trimbox_share), no personal data. The error log stays on your phone and goes into a feedback email only if you choose to include it.

See TrimBox privacy policy for details.

What it can't do

  • The nine vehicles other than the Sorento are estimated from specs and official cargo volumes and may differ from your car by a few centimeters. Some Sorento values, such as height and tailgate slope, are estimates too. Leave some room for tight fits.
  • Every item is treated as a box of its width, depth and height. Under-floor storage, SUVs with the 3rd row up and the luggage cover are not modeled.
  • It does not work out sleeping space inside the car, only the gear you load.
  • Weights are estimates from product data or typical values for the item type.
  • A layout holds up to 64 items.
  • TrimBox is an independent app, not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Kia, Hyundai or Tesla. Kia, Sorento, Carnival, Sportage, Ray, Hyundai, Santa Fe, Palisade, IONIQ, Casper, Tesla and Model Y are trademarks of their respective owners, used only to identify supported vehicles. Gear product names in the catalog are trademarks of their makers, used only to describe sizes, with no sponsorship or affiliation.

Frequently asked questions

How do I check whether all my camping gear fits?

Pick your gear and it is placed in the trunk right away. Tap Will it fit? to see whether the current layout fits, what is blocked and why, and how many items a repack would fit. It also checks whether the tailgate will close.

How close is it to my real car?

The Sorento is checked against published tape measurements, though a few values such as height and tailgate slope are estimates. The other nine vehicles are estimated from specs and official cargo volumes and may be off by a few centimeters. Treat the result as a guide, leave room for tight fits, and tell us at sugarmount21@gmail.com if a size looks wrong for your car.

Which cars does it support?

Kia Sorento (MQ4), Hyundai Santa Fe (MX5), Hyundai Palisade (LX3), Kia Carnival (KA4), Kia Sportage (NQ5), Tesla Model Y (2025+), Hyundai IONIQ 5 (2024+), Kia Ray, Hyundai Casper and Hyundai Casper Electric. For any other car, enter the trunk width, depth and height (wheel arches optional) to get a box shape. Ask for your car with Request a vehicle in the vehicle menu or in About.

Is it free?

It is free to install and shows ads. Vehicles, the check, auto-pack, the loading guide and the save & share card all work without paying. Named saves start with 1 slot and gain one more for each short ad you watch, up to 5.

What does Pro change?

With Pro (a one-time purchase), app open, rewarded and banner ads all stop showing, the card is made right away with no ad to watch, and named saves are unlimited. It is not a subscription, so nothing renews.

Are my layouts sent anywhere?

No. Layouts and their names stay on your phone, and we run no servers. The only data that leaves the device is the ad data the ads SDK sends to Google, the Google Play purchase and usage analytics with no layout content (Google Analytics); cards, layout files and emails leave only when you share or send them. The check and auto-pack work without internet.

When do ads appear?

Never while checking, packing or following the loading steps. An app open ad may appear when you come back after a while (max 2 a day), rewarded ads play only when you choose one for a card or a save slot, and there is a banner at the bottom of My layouts.

item.title: Our .gz Android assets hit FileNotFoundException – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

Our pre-gzipped level packs were each 18 bytes larger than the APK's own compressed copies, and the build dropped the trailing .gz, so the files could not be opened on the device.

A common trick for text data in an Android app's assets folder is to gzip it ahead of time to keep the APK small. In the 1,000-level update of our puzzle game Arrow Knots, five level packs shipped that way cost us twice: each was 18 bytes larger than the APK's own compressed copy, and the build stripped the trailing .gz from the names, so the app crashed with FileNotFoundException on its first launch.

When that crash hit a real phone (a Galaxy S21) on the night of October 3, 2026, every JVM test that read the same packs had passed. Below: the size measurement, why the tests missed it, and how to check your own APK.

705,234 bytes as gz files, 705,144 inside the APK

We opened the release APK built on October 28, 2026, read the raw and compressed size of each of the five level packs, and set them next to the .gz files the repository held until the fix. The pack contents haven't changed since, and each old .gz, decompressed, has the same SHA-1 as its plain pack, so these are the same bytes.

PackRawOld .gz fileCompressed in release APKDifference
p1 (1-200)122,96625,89625,87818
p2 (201-500)524,852111,113111,09518
p3 (501-700)679,344147,461147,44318
p4 (701-1000)1,397,319310,108310,09018
endless (1001-1100)492,814110,656110,63818
Total3,217,295705,234705,14490

Every pack differs by exactly 18 bytes. A gzip file wraps deflate data in a 10-byte header and an 8-byte trailer (CRC32 and original length), so the compressed bodies are the same size and the gap is the gzip wrapper. Don't pre-gzip text assets.

In the debug APK the same packs take 1,195,288 bytes, about 1.7 times the release figure. We haven't checked why. Measure asset sizes in a release APK.

The design's 4.4× compared the wrong pair

The case for gzip was one line in a design draft an agent wrote that afternoon: "300 levels = 535 KB raw / 121 KB gz (4.4×)", with an estimate of 0.7 to 0.85 MB gzipped for 1,000 levels. Raw sizes never ship, since the APK compresses the plain packs too. The pair to compare was the gz files against the plain packs as the APK compresses them.

The format went into the update spec committed at 17:18 that day. Several agents had cross-checked it, and it still put the packs in assets as .pack.gz and had the app read them with GZIPInputStream. At 18:32 the five packs were generated in that format, and the work of 41 agents (implementation, review and merges) finished at 22:27 with "none failed". Why that "done" meant JVM tests and a debug build is covered in How many AI coding agents can run at once?.

The APK listing had only arrows-p1.pack

The fresh-install monkey test caught it first; it ran because the operator's first request said to install on the S21 and run E2E. The script clears app data and sends 800 random events with seeds 7, 21 and 99. Seeds 7 and 21 each logged two fatal exceptions, and every one that made it into the log had the same message:

E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.RuntimeException: Unable to start activity
  ComponentInfo{…/sugar.arrows.MainActivity}:
  java.io.FileNotFoundException: arrows-p1.pack.gz

Thirty seconds later the agent listed the assets inside the debug APK. The source folder had arrows-p1.pack.gz at 25,896 bytes; the APK had assets/arrows-p1.pack at 122,966 bytes. All five packs looked like that: no .gz in the name, stored at their decompressed size. The commit message attributes this to aapt.

The tests opened the same files through a different function

The app and the tests share PackStore, the class that reads packs, but each passes in its own way to open a file. MainActivity uses PackStore(open = assets::open). ProgressTest uses PackStore(open = { FileInputStream(File(ASSETS, it)) }), where ASSETS is src/main/assets. The tests read the repository files as they are, so they see the .gz name and the gzip bytes. The generator module's test helper Shipped even carried the comment "read the way the app and tools read them". The app reads through AssetManager.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Plain packs, and what renaming the extension would have kept

At 22:31, the fix commit decompressed the packs into plain .pack files and removed GZIPInputStream from Levels.kt. The generator's writeGz became writePack, which writes text. The same commit deleted arrows-v2.pack (534,864 bytes), an old pack the app no longer read; two tests still did, and were moved to the new packs. Before the commit, 256 tests passed (engine 83, generator 40, app 133). At 22:34 the reinstalled app on the S21 had 0 fatal exceptions on all three monkey seeds and got through the tutorial to level 1.

Two other fixes were possible. Renaming the extension to something else would keep the build away from the name, so gzip could stay. But the table shows there is no size to gain, and all that would remain is GZIPInputStream plus the mtime-0 header the generator wrote to keep builds byte-identical. Keeping .gz in the source and having only the app open .pack would work on a device, but the tests would go on reading a different name and format than the app, which is how this crash got through. Neither alternative was tried in the repository; this comparison is our judgment while writing the note.

What the 19-line name test doesn't look at

The body of AssetNamesTest, added in the fix, is two statements. It was run before the fix and failed at 22:29 with no asset name ends in gz FAILED.

val gz = File("src/main/assets").listFiles().orEmpty().map { it.name }.filter { it.endsWith(".gz") }
assertTrue(gz.isEmpty(), "aapt renames these on install: $gz")

listFiles() doesn't descend into subfolders, so a file like assets/levels/x.gz slips past. Other source sets such as src/debug/assets, and the assets of the other app module in the same repository, aren't checked either. The "on install" in the message is also wrong: the APK listing showed .pack before anything was installed, so the rename happens at build time. We haven't confirmed which step of AGP 9.4.1 does it. The size result comes from 1,100 levels of text packs only; files that deflate can't shrink are outside it.

Checking asset names and sizes in your own APK

  1. Put the release APK listing next to the source folder: unzip -l app-release.apk | grep assets/ and ls src/main/assets. If names or counts differ, find the code that opens those files.
  2. Add a JVM test that fails on any asset name ending in .gz, and watch it fail before you fix anything. If you have subfolders, use walkTopDown().
  3. Decide whether to pre-compress from the compressed sizes inside the release APK. In Python, add up compress_size over zipfile.ZipFile(apk).infolist() and compare with your gz files.
  4. Open the first screen on a real device from a fresh install with app data cleared. The script is in the fresh-install monkey test note.

Still to do: .pack.gz left in the spec

As of October 29, 2026, the update spec still names .pack.gz five times, on four lines, and still says the packs are read with GZIPInputStream. The helper that reads the plain packs is still called Shipped.gzLines. When the spec gets fixed, we'll also decide how far AssetNamesTest should look.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does opening a .gz file from Android assets throw FileNotFoundException?

Because this project's build (AGP 9.4.1) dropped the trailing .gz and stored the file decompressed: the APK listing showed a decompressed x.pack instead of x.pack.gz. Open the name without .gz and drop GZIPInputStream.

Does pre-gzipping assets make the APK smaller?

Not for our 1,100 levels of text packs. The release APK's deflate came to 705,144 bytes; the pre-gzipped files were 705,234 bytes, larger by the 18-byte gzip header and trailer per pack.

Can a JVM unit test catch this kind of packaging problem?

It can enforce the naming rule. Whether AssetManager actually opens the file is only confirmed by running the app on a device or emulator.

Checked 2026-10-30. The game repository's git history, the monkey log and APK listing in that day's agent session record, and compressed sizes read with Python's zipfile from release and debug APKs built on October 28.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"
  • A launch crash only on Android 7: one java.time call in a shared module and a NewApi lint gate
  • Claude Code on WSL vs native Windows: what changed after the move
  • Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button: a 600 ms result-card lock, and the 28 crashes a stress run found next

item.title: "6.7" < "6.11" is false: a version string bug – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Incident

"6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates

Compare version strings with < and "6.7" comes out greater than "6.11". That is how our spelling app stopped delivering Remote Config content to devices with 6.2 to 6.9 stored.

Reworking a long-running spelling app 4/8

Storing an app or content version as a string like "6.7" and comparing it with < is common. It gives the right answer while the part after the dot has one digit, then silently gives the wrong one at 6.10. In SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling app, that comparison kept the quiz bank and notices sent through Remote Config from reaching some devices. It surfaced on September 25, 2026, when the operator held the 6.7 shown in a device's drawer up against the 6.11 on the server. Below: the cause, three agent commits that walked past the check, the replacement function, and how to verify the fix on an existing install.

The drawer said 6.7; Remote Config said 6.11

The app ships its quiz bank, notices and FAQ as one JSON value in Firebase Remote Config (RC below). On the splash screen, ActivityEmpty compares RC's info_version and clip_version with the version stored in the device's Room database. If RC is newer, it deletes the local content and inserts the new set. The (6.7/2.2) at the bottom of the drawer is that stored version.

One suspect was the build. Debug builds of this app read the RC of a separate development Firebase project, so a debug build on the device could show numbers that differ from production. Production RC really was 6.11/2.3, which ruled that out and left the comparison code.

// ActivityEmpty, just before the fix
if (res[0].infoVersion < infoVer || res[0].clipVersion < clipVer) {
    repo.setVersion(VersionT(infoVer, clipVer))
    // delete and re-insert content
}

infoVersion is a String field. Kotlin compares strings lexicographically, character by character, so "6.7" and "6.11" first differ at the third character: '7' against '1'. '7' is larger, "6.7" < "6.11" evaluates to false, and the app concluded that RC held the older version.

With one digit after the dot, both orders agree

String comparison has been there since the app first connected to Remote Config in 2020. The current form, infoVersion < infoVer, appeared on May 6, 2023, when a commit flipped the comparison to the right direction; the clip condition was added two days later. While the minor part ran from 6.1 to 6.9, lexicographic order and numeric order were the same, and the check always gave the right answer. It broke when RC moved to 6.10. We recomputed what the old expression returns for each stored value:

Stored on the deviceRC at 6.10RC at 6.11
6.1updatesupdates
6.2 to 6.9skipsskips
6.10equalupdates

"6.1" is a prefix of "6.10", so the shorter string sorts first; 6.2 through 6.9 all win at the third character. From the day RC reached 6.10, a device stuck in that range ignored every info_version bump (unless clip_version also went up). The quiz bank review document also records that notices changed on September 13, 20 and 22 without any change to info_version, which stayed at 6.10. Those three notices reached no existing user, string comparison or not.

Fresh installs never showed the bug. On first run there is no stored version row, so the app inserts the RC content without comparing anything and starts on the latest set.

Three agent commits, none of them fixed the content check

Counting only the times an agent touched or reasoned about the version check itself, the git history shows three. On August 9, 2025 at 15:32, a commit generated with Claude Code blamed a "persistent update notice" on the string comparison of app_version and switched major, minor and patch to integer comparison. The app was at 1.5.031, so major and minor were one character each and the string comparison gave the same answer anyway. At 17:51 that day a commit whose message just says "fix" put the string comparison back. No reason was recorded. Neither commit touched the content version check.

On December 11, 2025, an RC sync refactor (co-authored by Claude Opus 4.5) added 11 tests (its message says 13). One of them, versionComparison_isCorrect, asserts that "5.0" < "5.1". It uses single-digit values and calls no app code, only Kotlin's String operator, so it passes whatever the production check does. How we find tests that stay green when the guarded code is deleted is in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database.

On the morning of September 25, 2026, the agent reviewing all 124 quiz items (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote into the publishing steps of its 11:08 commit: the splash screen compares versions as strings, so bump info_version to 7.0. Fifteen minutes later the value that went up was 6.11, and the document now said that 6.10 to 6.11 is larger even as a string, so 6.10 users would update. The document still said a 6.9 to 6.10 bump is not recognized, but said nothing about what to do for devices stuck below 6.10. The 11:23 commit also added a rule to the project's agent instruction file (CLAUDE.md), that a bump which changes the number of digits is not seen as an update, and left the comparison code as it was.

Devices below 6.10 surfaced only when the operator put the drawer's 6.7/2.2 next to production RC. The 12:14 fix was also written by an agent (Claude Fable 5.1), this time after the operator had pointed out that the device and RC values differed. How this incident shows up in the commit messages is covered, along with other cases, in A year of AI coding in 701 commits.

One VersionCompare for both content and app versions

Setting RC to 7.0 would have unblocked 6.x devices for now, since "6.x" < "7.0" is true. It would break again at 7.10, and everyone editing content would have to remember never to make a bump that adds a digit, so we dropped it as a permanent rule.

Comparing all three parts as integers, as in August 2025, did not fit either. This app looks only at the major and minor parts of app_version and ignores the patch on purpose; comparing the patch would send every user on an older patch to the store after each patch release. The 12:14 fix keeps one function and routes both the content version check and the major/minor checks of app_version through it.

object VersionCompare {
    fun compare(a: String, b: String): Int {
        val pa = parts(a); val pb = parts(b)
        for (i in 0 until maxOf(pa.size, pb.size)) {
            val x = pa.getOrElse(i) { 0 }; val y = pb.getOrElse(i) { 0 }
            if (x != y) return x.compareTo(y)
        }
        return 0
    }
    fun isNewer(remote: String, local: String) = compare(remote, local) > 0
    private fun parts(v: String) = v.trim().split('.').map { it.trim().toIntOrNull() ?: 0 }
}

The four tests in VersionCompareTest cover the values that failed ("6.11" against "6.7"), equal values, parts of different lengths or counts ("1.10.0" against "1.9.9", "6.11" against "6.11.0") and non-numeric input. The first test also asserts that "6.7" < "6.11" is false. 112 unit tests passed at that commit. Do not write a new version check with a string <; that rule is in CLAUDE.md now.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The force flag in the same JSON went on before adoption

The RC version JSON that holds the content versions also holds app_version and force, and since that fix the major/minor check of app_version goes through VersionCompare too. The splash screen decides in this order: if the installed version matches app_version character for character, let the user in; otherwise compare major and minor only; finally, if force is true, override the result and show the update dialog.

A September 18 note records that a device with 1.6.017 showed "A new version has been released!", and the code was the first suspect. The real cause was an RC app_version that did not match the shipped version. A patch bump (1.6.017 to 1.6.018) is not rescued by the major/minor check, so the dialog goes away only when the RC value matches the shipped version exactly.

On that same September 18, force went on while few users had the new version, and sessions for the day were down 25% five hours later. A September 13 case is left out here: a note written that day corrected an earlier reading as GA4 standard-report lag rather than a lockout, while later documents list it as a lockout again. Since 1.6.019 (September 19), our monitoring script reads the RC version JSON and prints, from GA4 for yesterday and today, the share of active users on exactly the app_version string. If force is true and that share is under 90%, it warns that the rest are stuck behind the splash dialog right now. A separate rollout incident, where a staged percentage went out wrong, is in A 20% staged rollout went out at 100%.

One git grep, a test with the failing values, a check on an old install

  1. Find lines that compare version-like names with < or >. Run on our revision from before the fix, it found the two lines in the splash screen and three in the December 2025 test (run on 2026-10-29). 
    git grep -nE '[Vv]er[A-Za-z]*(\[[0-9]\])?\s*[<>]=?\s*[A-Za-z.\[]*[Vv]er' -- '*.kt' '*.java'
  2. Move every hit into one function and test it with the values that failed. At minimum: "6.11" against "6.7" and "1.10.0" against "1.9.9".
  3. Do not verify on a fresh install. Install the build from before the fix and run it once with RC at 6.9 so the stored version is 6.9. Install the fixed build over it without clearing data, raise RC to 6.10, and check that the stored version shown on screen becomes 6.10. A bump that keeps the digit count, such as 6.15 to 6.16, passes under the old comparison too and proves nothing.
  4. When content changes, bump info_version.
  5. Before turning force on, check in GA4 the share of active users whose appVersion equals the RC app_version. Under 90%, leave it off.

Builds already installed still compare strings

The comparison runs on the device, so a device that has not updated to the fixed build keeps comparing strings. RC has since gone to 6.12 (October 1), 6.13 (October 9), 6.14 (October 10) and 6.15 (October 24), but on an old build with 6.2 to 6.9 stored, "6.7" < "6.15" is still false.

One server-side way to reach those devices is a one-time bump of the RC value to 7.0. On old builds "6.7" < "7.0" is true, and on new builds VersionCompare also sees 7.0 as newer than 6.15, so both paths update. We dropped 7.0 as a permanent rule, but as a one-time migration while old builds remain it is the right tool; after it, bumps should stay within 7.1 to 7.9 until old builds are rare enough. As of October 24 the RC value is 6.15, and there is no record of this app moving to 7.0. Because the old condition is an OR, raising clip_version would also make it true, but we do not know why those devices did not update at clip 2.3, so we do not count that path as a confirmed fix.

VersionCompare reads any non-numeric part as 0. A typo such as "6.l1" in RC would read as 6.0 and the update would be skipped silently; the test only confirms that "6.7" is newer than "abc" and raises no warning. "6.11" and "6.11.0" count as the same version.

For 1.6.023 a release APK on an API 34 emulator showed 6.11/2.3 in the drawer, but the record does not say whether that was a fresh install. If it was, the check never ran. clip_version is an open question too: stored 2.2, RC 2.3. "2.2" < "2.3" is true even as strings and the old condition was an OR, so the clip side should have triggered an update. The history does not say when clip became 2.3, so string comparison alone does not fully explain why this device stayed at 6.7/2.2.

Writing the version row before the content was another defect on the same update path. On September 28, on a physical S21, a first run while offline left the quiz bank empty until the next info_version; a fix now refills the bank when it is empty even if the version matches.

The old rule is still in the instruction file

As of October 29, 2026, the app's agent instruction file (CLAUDE.md) still says in one place that the comparison is a string comparison and a bump that adds a digit is not seen as an update, and says in another that versions are compared numerically with VersionCompare. An agent that reads the first rule could believe the code still compares strings and pick bump values to suit it. The old sentence should become the one-time 7.0 migration rule for old builds, and "always bump info_version" stays. versionComparison_isCorrect, which calls no app code, is also still in the test suite. When you fix code like this, fix the instruction file's old description in the same commit.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Reworking a long-running spelling app: all 8 parts

  1. A month of 'temporary error': our subscription details screen never waited for products, and 1 of 16 users started checkout
  2. A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop

FAQ

Why is "6.7" < "6.11" false in Kotlin?

String comparison is lexicographic, character by character. At the third character '7' is greater than '1', so "6.7" sorts after "6.11".

Wouldn't bumping the version to 7.0 work with string comparison?

For now, yes. It breaks again at 7.10, and everyone editing content has to avoid bumps that add a digit.

When is it safe to turn on Remote Config's force flag?

Once at least 90% of active users run exactly the app_version string. This app turned it on with low adoption and lost 25% of the day's sessions.

Sources: the app repository's git history, CHANGELOG entries 1.6.019 and 1.6.023, the quiz bank review document and the monitoring script, rechecked on 2026-10-29. Remote Config template numbers and project identifiers are left out.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Play Billing subscription screen 'temporary error' – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

A month of 'temporary error': our subscription details screen never waited for products, and 1 of 16 users started checkout

A "temporary error" on a subscription screen may not be Play's fault. Our details screen decided the product list was empty before Play Billing had answered, and sent users away.

Reworking a long-running spelling app 3/8

When an Android app opens its subscription screen, it asks the Play Billing Library for product details, and the answer arrives a moment later. Our spell checker's details screen did not wait for it: it checked the list right away, and over 90 days only 1 of the 16 users who reached the screen started checkout. This note follows one Play review to the cause, the fix (wait up to 8 seconds), the seven billing defects found after it, and a checklist for your own subscription screen.

The 90-day funnel: 45 on the plans screen, 16 on details, 1 at checkout

On September 26 we pulled the subscription events for our Korean spell checker, SugarSpeller, counted by user, over 90 days. 45 users saw the plans screen, 16 went on to the details screen where you pick a billing period, and 1 started checkout. Fifteen of the sixteen (94%) left the details screen without starting a purchase. The details-screen events split 18 premium and 2 basic, spread across seven versions between 1.6.016 and 1.6.024.

It started with a review with 18 "helpful" votes: trying to subscribe to premium gave a "temporary error", and had for a month. That "temporary error" is the app's generic retry toast, which in Korean reads roughly "A temporary error occurred. Please try again."

The function that requested products judged an empty list one line later

addSubsItems() on the details screen launched a coroutine in lifecycleScope that waited on the product flow with firstOrNull(), and then, further down the same function, checked the list size straight away. Trimmed, the old code looked like this:

getProductDetails(repo.premiumProductDetails)   // inside: launch { flow.firstOrNull() }
if (recyclerAdapterSubscription!!.mItemList!!.size <= 0) {
    Toast.makeText(..., R.string.string_common_error_retry, ...).show()
    startActivity(main screen)
}

If the billing manager's StateFlow already held the product, firstOrNull() returned on the spot and the list filled. If not, the coroutine suspended, the function moved on, and the size check saw an empty list. Every user whose products were not already cached got the toast and landed back on the main screen. The size check came in with a commit on January 4, 2024; the firstOrNull() call with one on October 3, 2024.

The September 26 fix turned the check into a wait. The screen now shows a progress dialog and waits inside withTimeoutOrNull(8_000); only if nothing arrives in 8 seconds does it show the toast and go back. The code comment gives the reasoning: connecting to billing and querying products usually takes 1 to 2 seconds, so wait several times that. We did not measure a latency distribution to pick 8 seconds.

The 2024 belief that Play 'sometimes splits the response' came from our own for loop

BillingClientManager stored the products Play returned only if(newMap.size >= 2), that is, only when basic and premium arrived in the same response. The commit that added the line, on October 4, 2024, says the product details response "intermittently comes in separately or together", so only store it when both arrive at once.

The split came from the app. Since December 30, 2023, queryProductDetails() had called queryProductDetailsAsync inside the loop that built the product list, once per iteration. With two products, that sent a one-product query and then a two-product query, and the responses came back as a one-item list and a two-item list. The 2024 fix hid the symptom by throwing away the one-item response. In exchange, whenever Play returned only one product (for example when one product's base plan is turned off), the map stayed empty for good.

The same fix queries once and merges whatever arrives into the existing map. In Play Billing Library 9.1.0, QueryProductDetailsResult reports products Play could not return in unfetchedProductList; we now log it, which separates Play Console setup problems from app problems.

Three of the agent's first five tests stopped at Mockito

The fix was made with an AI coding agent (Claude Code), tests first: three Robolectric screen tests (waits while products are missing, lists plans when they arrive late, errors only when they never arrive) and two billing manager tests (single-product response, split responses merged). All five failed on the first run, but three of them were not reproducing the bug:

java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "org.mockito.plugins.MockMaker$TypeMockability.mockable()" because "typeMockability" is null

The agent had mocked ProductDetails with Mockito. The class is final, and this project's test classpath mixes in mockito-android, so final mocks could not be created, and we dropped the mock. ProductDetails has a package-private constructor that takes a JSON string, so a test helper, TestProductDetails, lives under the same package name, com.android.billingclient.api, and builds real objects from the JSON shape Play sends (productId, type, subscriptionOfferDetails, pricingPhases). On the next run all five failed for the intended reasons: the screen test with "sent the user to main even though products simply had not arrived yet", the merge test expecting basic and premium and getting an empty set. After the fix they passed. A trimmed version of the helper, with product IDs and price replaced by placeholders:

package com.android.billingclient.api   // test sources; the constructor is package-private
fun subscriptionMonthly(productId: String, basePlanId: String): ProductDetails {
    val phase = JSONObject().put("priceAmountMicros", 1_000_000_000).put("priceCurrencyCode", "KRW")
        .put("formattedPrice", "KRW 1,000").put("billingPeriod", "P1M").put("recurrenceMode", 1)
    val offer = JSONObject().put("basePlanId", basePlanId).put("offerIdToken", "token-$basePlanId")
        .put("offerTags", JSONArray()).put("pricingPhases", JSONArray().put(phase))
    val json = JSONObject().put("productId", productId).put("type", "subs")
        .put("title", productId).put("name", productId).put("description", "test")
        .put("subscriptionOfferDetails", JSONArray().put(offer))
    return ProductDetails(json.toString())     // a real object, not a mock
}
// usage: subscriptionMonthly("premium", "premium-monthly")

On a Galaxy S21 the screen still bounced, and a rebuild from the Sep 26 evening code did the same

On September 28 we opened the details screen on a Galaxy S21. The progress indicator spun, the screen closed, and the app went back to main. The first suspect was the changes from the past two days, so we built a release APK from the Sep 26 evening code (which already had the wait fix) and installed it on the same phone. It failed the same way, after 8 seconds. The billing connection's error was In-app billing API version 3 is not supported, and the phone's Google Play services build was from December 2024.

The phone was the cause, but two app defects showed up with it. When billing setup ended in failure, no disconnect callback followed, so nothing ever reconnected; until the app was restarted, the screen waited the full 8 seconds every time and then showed a "please try again" that had nothing to do with the cause. The same day we made the billing manager expose a connection state (connecting, ready, or unavailable with a response code). In 1.6.025 the wait looks like this:

repo.ensureConnected()                       // reconnect if an earlier attempt failed
popupDialog.showDialog(POPUP_TYPE.PROGRESS, true)
lifecycleScope.launch {
    val outcome: Any? = try {
        withTimeoutOrNull(PRODUCT_LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS) {   // 8_000L
            merge(source, repo.connectionState.filterIsInstance<BillingConnectionState.Unavailable>())
                .firstOrNull()                        // products or a failed connection, whichever comes first
        }
    } finally { popupDialog.stopDialog() }
    // Unavailable: (on BILLING/SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE) "check the Play Store" + subscription_unavailable / null (over 8 s): retry toast / else: list the plans
}

On BILLING_UNAVAILABLE it skips the wait, tells the user to check the Play Store, and sends a subscription_unavailable event to GA4.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The day after 'ready to ship', the operator's own test on an S23 led to seven more billing defects

On September 29, version 1.6.025 was logged as ready to ship (the review process that day is in How to trust an AI agent's code review). The next morning the operator installed the latest build on a Galaxy S23, tried subscribing, reported that it was not working, and said the release could not go out like this. That prompted another round on the S21 with agent cross-checking: three analysis agents, two refutation passes, three fix agents and two adversarial reviews. It found seven billing defects that had been in the app since 1.6.024 or earlier:

  1. When the purchase sheet failed immediately, the progress indicator never went away, and a background thread kept one CPU core busy.
  2. The billing setup callback wrote OK into the same global value as purchase results, which read as "subscription complete".
  3. A PENDING purchase was treated as a success.
  4. Every return to the app created a new BillingClient (a leak), and the Classic screen saw an empty purchase list before the query finished and saved subscribers as free users.
  5. The Chat screen did not apply benefits after a purchase.
  6. Starting checkout without knowing the current purchases let an existing subscriber buy a second subscription.
  7. A screen's onDestroy closed the billing connection the whole app shared.

The September 30 fixes moved purchase results into their own flow, separate from connection state, and read purchases from a signal that fills only after a successful query, so a user is downgraded only when the query succeeded and found no active subscription. Checkout now re-queries purchases right before it starts and does not open the purchase sheet when they are unknown. Counting every fix that day, unit tests went from 250 to 292.

We never read the S23's logs, but the same test on the S21 showed the problem was how we were testing. A sideloaded release build that was never uploaded to Play gets Play's "Google Play billing is not available for this version" message, and the debug build, whose package name ends in .debug, has no products registered in Play. The only way to run a real purchase end to end is to upload to the internal testing track and install from Play with a license tester account, so that check became a step in the release procedure.

Judge now, wait forever, or wait 8 seconds

Judging right away, the old behavior, treats "the list is empty the moment the screen opens" as an error, so it went. Waiting forever was already half there in the old code: firstOrNull() never returns if the product never comes, so deleting only the size check would have left users staring at an empty screen. We also wrote down the next move in case the 8-second wait was the wrong fix: if checkout starts from details were still 0 to 10% 30 days after release, the product query itself is failing, and the next step is retrying the billing connection.

Do not judge asynchronously loaded product details the moment the screen opens. Set a ceiling on the wait, and when the failure already has a known cause, such as an unavailable billing connection, report it right away instead of waiting. The same two rules now sit in the subscription section of the agent instructions (CLAUDE.md) in this app's repository.

4 of 13 is an interim number, and device-side billing failures stay

The other half of the September 26 rule: 30 days after release, if more than 30% of details-screen users start checkout, the cause is confirmed. The interim 31% on October 17 clears the bar, and two purchases went through, but it rests on 13 users. A log entry on October 18 found that Play's pre-launch robots had inflated version 1.6.030's subscription screen numbers; whether any of these 13 were robots is not recorded. (How we filter those devices in GA4 is in GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real.)

On the same day, subscription_unavailable fired for 2 of the 13 (15%). Users whose device cannot bill, through outdated Play services or a sign-in problem, are still there after the fix, and the most the app can do is say so clearly. We have only used TestProductDetails with Play Billing Library 9.1.0, and the Robolectric tests never see a real purchase or Play's signature check.

Checking whether your own subscription screen turns users away

  1. Put the plans-screen, details-screen and checkout-start events side by side in GA4, counted by user. If checkout starts from details are in single-digit percent, open the details screen code first.
  2. In any function that launches a collector on the product flow, look for a list-size check further down the same function.
  3. Check whether queryProductDetailsAsync runs inside a loop and whether the response handler stores products only when all of them arrive. Merge what arrives, and log unfetchedProductList.
  4. Have the details screen wait with a progress indicator and a ceiling, and end immediately with a "update Play" message when billing setup finishes with BILLING_UNAVAILABLE or SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE.
  5. Create a com.android.billingclient.api package in your test sources with a helper that builds ProductDetails from JSON. Make the three screen cases (waiting, late arrival, never arrives) and the two manager cases (single and split responses) fail first, then fix.
  6. Verify real purchases through the internal testing track and a license tester.
  7. Before release, write down the decision rule with a date: above what rate the cause is confirmed, below what rate it is something else.

What the October 31 check has to answer

The final check is due on October 31, 30 days after 1.6.025 shipped. First we check for pre-launch robots among the details-screen users. Then we look at two numbers: checkout starts against the 30% line, and subscription_unavailable against 5%, above which a button that goes straight to the Play Store is on the table. The records do not show whether the internal-track real purchase check we added to the release procedure was done before 1.6.025 shipped.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Reworking a long-running spelling app: all 8 parts

  1. Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%
  2. "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates

Frequently asked questions

My subscription screen keeps showing a "temporary error". Is Google Play down?

Check your own code first. Our details screen decided the product list was empty before the asynchronous product details arrived, and sent every user without cached products away. If retrying always gives the same result, it is not a temporary outage.

How do I test with ProductDetails when Mockito cannot mock it?

Create the com.android.billingclient.api package in your test sources and call the package-private constructor with JSON shaped like Play's response, which gives you a real object. We ran five tests this way on Play Billing Library 9.1.0.

Is "Google Play billing is not available for this version" on a sideloaded APK a bug?

No. Builds that were never uploaded to Play, and debug packages, cannot bill. Upload to the internal testing track and install from Play with a license tester account to check a real purchase.

Sources: the app repository's git history and CHANGELOG (September 26 and 30, 2026), the monitoring log, and work session logs from September 26 to 30. User counts are GA4 users.

item.title: Android 16 KB page size, NDK 27 and a blue tint – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Android 16 KB page size: add the linker flag before you upgrade the NDK (NDK 27 and 29 tinted our photos blue)

Play's 16 KB page requirement was met with one linker flag, even on NDK 25. The NDK upgrade we made first is what put a blue tint on photo transitions.

Google Play requires apps targeting Android 15 or later to ship native libraries (.so files) aligned for 16 KB memory pages. In SugarAlbum, our app that turns photos into videos, the six arm64 libraries we build ourselves were 4 KB aligned (0x1000). In January 2026, working with an AI coding agent, we moved to NDK 26.3, added a linker flag and got them to 16 KB (0x4000). Along the way, builds made with NDK 27.0 and 29.0 put a blue cast on photo transitions.

On October 27, 2026 we rebuilt the same source with four NDK versions, and NDK 25.1, which our records called "16KB unsupported", gave 0x4000 once the linker flag was in. The upgrade was never needed. Below are the commands to measure alignment, the RELRO check that is easy to miss, and an order of checks to follow.

The three .so files rebuilt for targetSdk 36 were still 4 KB aligned

As of January 2026 SugarAlbum has 763 Java files and 32 Kotlin files, and the video and filter work runs in C/C++ libraries built with ndk-build. We raised targetSdk from 33 to 34 in July 2024 and from 34 to 36 at the end of August 2025. On August 31, 2025 we rebuilt the three arm64 libraries of the multimediaFramework module (libBeatTracker, libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils) without telling the linker about page size, and the other three (libnative_filter, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer) were still the November 2022 builds. So right before the January work, all six had LOAD segments aligned to 0x1000.

Google announced on the Android Developers Blog on May 8, 2025 that starting November 1, 2025, new apps and updates targeting Android 15 or higher must support 16 KB pages. The current page size guide (updated 2026-10-16) says that starting February 1, 2027, updates without 16 KB support can't be released. Our repo notes say a Play Console warning asked for a fix "by May 2025". That date appears in neither official source, and the warning text itself isn't saved anywhere in the repo.

The January work was done with Claude Code; the commit carries its Co-Authored-By line. A work note committed alongside it records the first move: "After: NDK 27.0.12077973. Reason: the APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES flag is only supported in NDK r27 and later." The final commit used 26.3, and the work note went in still saying 27.0.

NDK 27.0 and 29.0 builds tinted photo transitions blue

The commit message has a three-line NDK table: 25.x does not support 16 KB, 26.3 works (adopted), 27.0 and 29.0 show "a blue tint bug with -O3 optimization". A work note in the same commit describes the symptom as a bluish cast during photo transitions, places it in the PixelUtils and libyuv code of the multimediaFramework module, and notes that an -O0 build looks normal. All five modules in that module's Android.mk (libYUV, libMasp, PixelCanvas, PixelUtils, BeatTracker) compile with -O3.

No automated check caught it. The only tests in the repo are the two placeholder tests Android Studio generates (ExampleUnitTest and ExampleInstrumentedTest); nothing compares colors or rendered frames. NDK 27.0 and 29.0 both built cleanly and both produced aligned libraries. The tint showed up only when someone ran the app and watched a transition.

The work note names the cause as "a Clang -O3 optimization bug". The only evidence on record is that -O0 looks fine. The bundled compilers are clang 17.0.2 in NDK 26.3, 18.0.1 in 27.0 and 21.0.0 in 29.0, so the tint lines up with clang 18 and later. A clean -O0 build is also what you'd see if our own code had undefined behavior that the newer optimizer treats differently, and nobody narrowed it down to a function.

The same commit tidied the libyuv NEON lines in Android.mk, so we checked that too. libPixelUtils.so exports 198 symbols with NEON in the name both before and after the commit. The NEON code was already in the old build, so it isn't the variable.

NDK 26.3 ignores APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES

The final commit sets alignment in three places: android.ndk.maxPageSize=16384 in gradle.properties, APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES := true in three Application.mk files, and LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in six Android.mk modules. To see which one did the work, we searched each NDK's build/core for the flag name. It isn't in 25.1 or 26.3; it's only in build-binary.mk of 27.0 and 29.0. In 27.0, a true value adds max-page-size=16384 to the link. In 29.0, 16 KB is the default and a false value sets it back to 4096.

Then we rebuilt the libnative_filter source from the January commit (two C files) with each NDK and read the LOAD alignment with llvm-readelf -lW on 2026-10-27.

NDKLinker flag in Android.mkarm64-v8a LOAD alignment
25.1.8937393no0x1000
25.1.8937393yes0x4000
26.3.11579264no (Application.mk flag only)0x1000
26.3.11579264yes (as committed)0x4000
27.0.12077973no (Application.mk flag only)0x4000
29.0.14206865no0x4000

Under 26.3 the 16 KB alignment came from the Android.mk linker flag; the Application.mk line did nothing. The same flag gave 0x4000 under 25.1. The commit's "NDK 25.x: 16KB unsupported" was never tested with the flag in place, and it follows from the first assumption that the feature needs r27. The official guide's "Android NDK r27 and lower" section also gets 16 KB alignment from the max-page-size and common-page-size linker flags and never mentions APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES.

The six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries pass the LOAD check and fail the RELRO formula

The work note left six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries (libavcodec-56, libavfilter-5, libavformat-56, libavutil-54, libswresample-1, libswscale-3) marked as needing a separate 16 KB rebuild. Their LOAD segments were already aligned to 0x10000 (64 KB) before the commit. 64 KB is a multiple of 16 KB, so they pass the guide's rule that no LOAD segment may be below 2**14.

The guide has a second check. (VirtAddr + MemSiz) of the GNU_RELRO segment should divide evenly by 0x4000. If it doesn't, and RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data that follows it (.data, .bss), the app can crash at runtime with a segmentation fault. A LOAD segment holding only RELRO data, followed by a writable LOAD that starts on a separate 16 KB page, is a case where the formula doesn't apply; the guide's example of that layout is still 16 KB compliant. We ran all twelve arm64 libraries from the January commit through that formula.

LibraryRELRO end % 0x4000Result
libnative_filter, libBeatTracker, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer0x0pass
libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils0x1000formula doesn't apply (RELRO-only LOAD)
six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries0x1000 to 0x3000RELRO shares a LOAD with .data/.bss

In libavcodec-56, the writable LOAD segment is 0x257f00 bytes in memory and only its first 0xfbf8 bytes are RELRO, which is the shape the guide uses as its crash example. The commit added only max-page-size; the guide's examples also pass common-page-size=16384. Our six self-built libraries passed without it. The repo has FFmpeg's source and build scripts, but nothing records which flags produced the .so files it ships. The work note says -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 was added to both build scripts; in this commit the scripts were only moved, and their linker flag variable (ADDI_LDFLAGS) doesn't have that flag.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Keeping NDK 25.1 and adding the linker flag would have worked

There were three ways to go in January. We pinned NDK 26.3 and wrote "do not use NDK 27 or later" into the notes.

  • Stay on NDK 25.1 and add the linker flag. The table above says alignment would have been fine, and since the records show no tint on 25.1 and the compiler would have stayed the same, there was no reason to expect a color regression. It was ruled out by the "25 unsupported" call.
  • Use NDK 27 or 29 and lower -O3 only in multimediaFramework. -O0 is recorded as looking fine, but nobody measured how much slower video processing gets.
  • Find and fix the function that shifts the color. There's no record of an attempt.

Don't upgrade the NDK first. Put the linker flag into the NDK you already use and check the alignment with readelf. If you have another reason to move to a newer NDK, do it as a separate change and compare rendered output against the previous build.

CMake builds and NDK r28 or later need a different procedure

This is an ndk-build project (Android.mk, Application.mk). With CMake, the guide puts the flags in target_link_options, and the Android.mk line is irrelevant. NDK r28 and later align to 16 KB by default, so the flag isn't needed at all; our 29.0 build gave 0x4000 on arm64 with no flag.

There's no basis for saying NDK 27 will do the same to other code. We didn't check 32-bit (armeabi-v7a) libraries; the guide's requirement covers 64-bit devices.

Checking with readelf twice and the same set of photos

  1. For each arm64-v8a .so that ships in the APK or AAB, read the LOAD alignment. The last column must be 0x4000 or larger.
    llvm-readelf -lW libfoo.so | grep -E "LOAD|GNU_RELRO"
  2. If there's a GNU_RELRO line, add VirtAddr and MemSiz and take the remainder mod 0x4000. If it isn't zero, check whether the LOAD segment holding RELRO also holds .data/.bss (its MemSiz is much larger than RELRO's).
  3. Before changing the NDK, add both flags from the guide to Android.mk in your current NDK and repeat step 1.
    LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384
  4. APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES is read only by NDK r27 and later. On r26 or older, that line alone does nothing.
  5. Delete the .so files in jniLibs and rebuild every time you change the NDK or the flags. Our notes record that Android Studio's Clean Project doesn't remove jniLibs, so the build script deletes them first.
  6. Export a video from the same photos with the old build and the new one, and watch the transitions side by side.
  7. If you ship uncompressed .so files, confirm Android Gradle Plugin 8.5.1 or later and run zipalign -v -c -P 16 4 app.apk. SugarAlbum uses AGP 8.12.0.

Another Play Console warning we traced is in Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used. The app itself is on the SugarAlbum page.

Not done yet: a 16 KB emulator run and a per-module -O3 check

Video export has to run end to end on a 16 KB page emulator image to see whether the FFmpeg libraries crash on RELRO. If they do, FFmpeg needs a rebuild with common-page-size=16384. We still don't know which module the tint comes from; one way to narrow it down is to take the five multimediaFramework modules off -O3 one at a time. The NDK 27.0 in the work note should be corrected to 26.3.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do I need NDK r27 or later to support 16 KB pages?

Not for the alignment itself. With -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in Android.mk, NDK 25.1 rebuilt libnative_filter.so (arm64) with 0x4000 LOAD alignment (measured 2026-10-27). r27 is only needed for the one-line APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES approach.

How do I check whether a .so is 16 KB aligned?

Run llvm-readelf -lW or llvm-objdump -p and confirm every LOAD segment is aligned to 0x4000 (2**14) or more. If GNU_RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data, also check that (VirtAddr + MemSiz) % 0x4000 is zero.

Can I keep a prebuilt .so that is 64 KB aligned?

It passes the LOAD alignment check. SugarAlbum's six FFmpeg libraries are 0x10000 and pass that check, but their RELRO remainders are 0x1000 to 0x3000.

Checked 2026-10-27. SugarAlbum git history and work notes, .so alignment rechecked with llvm-readelf, and the official Android Developers documentation.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"
  • 4.5:1 contrast in the site build: the dark hover pair that failed for 7 of 11 apps

item.title: AI app design review: 3 agent designs, 3 judges – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · How-to

Three agent designs, three judges: the market judge alone would have picked the one that crashed on every KakaoTalk file

Use at least three design judges with different viewpoints and pick the winner by total score. With only our market-veteran judge, the winning design would have crashed on every file opened from KakaoTalk.

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer 1/8

If you have AI agents write competing designs and other agents grade them, who sits on the panel decides the winner. Before writing any code for SugarDoc, our Android viewer for HWP, HWPX and PDF documents, we had three designs that differed only in priority scored by three judges with different viewpoints. The market judge's favorite would have crashed every time someone opened a document received in KakaoTalk; the Android-engineer and policy judges caught it. All of this happened in 59 minutes before any code existed, and the crashing entry point never reached the repository.

59 minutes before any code: research, refutation, three designs, judging, critique

HWP and HWPX are the file formats of Hangul, the word processor Korean schools and government offices use, and many people receive these files through KakaoTalk, Korea's dominant messenger. On the evening of October 4 we had market research and an engine spike for a viewer (the engine numbers are in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents) and zero lines of code. At 21:34 KST the main session wrote one Claude Code Workflow script and started it.

The script has five stages. Twelve agents research twelve areas separately: competitors, the HWP engine, the PDF engine, intents and entry, the received-documents inbox, monetization, UX, the codebase, store search, quality, security and scope. Two reviewers per area then try to break each report. Any finding that at least one of the 24 verification reports marked refuted was deleted before design; there were 16. From what remained, three design agents wrote designs that differ only in priority, three judges scored them, and one critic checked the final plan made from the winner plus ideas grafted from the others. A last agent was assigned five documents: analysis, PRD, screen contract, architecture and implementation plan.

In all, 45 agents used 8.8 million tokens in 59 minutes. Research ran from minute 0 to 16 and verification, starting on each area as soon as its research finished, from 7 to 26. The three designs took 6 minutes, judging two and a half, and synthesis, critique and document writing 25.

The three design prompts differed by one sentence

Every agent got the same shared context: the repository layout (minSdk 29, targetSdk 36), where the earlier research lived, the goal, a rule to tag each claim as verified, inferred or unverified, and a ban on editing files, installing packages, committing or touching devices. Each stage returned JSON against a fixed schema.

StageGist of the instructionOutput
VerifyOne reviewer always fact-checks: if you cannot reproduce the evidence yourself, default to refuted or uncertain. The other takes an area lens: market, feasibility, Android platform, policy or userconfirmed/refuted/uncertain per finding, keep/change/drop per recommendation, what is missing
DesignUse only the verified dossier, answer the reviewers' pushback, never build the design on an uncertain finding without a validation step; one priority sentence (speed, quality or growth)scope, architecture, screens, quality gates, milestones with day estimates, risks
JudgeOne persona. Score 0 to 10 on win potential, feasibility, reliability, revenue and policy safety. Be harsh, find fatal flaws, pick a winner, list ideas to graftscores, winner, grafts, fatal flaws
CritiqueDoes every release feature have a milestone and a test, every risk a mitigation or validation task? Are the ad rules enforced by tests? Are estimates realistic for one developer plus Claude? Are human-only tasks listed?each gap rated blocker, major or minor, with a fix

The three priority sentences: speed, "reach the internal track in two to three weeks, inside the October demand window, without giving up never-fails-to-open and no ads on documents"; quality, "open everything correctly and fast on low-end phones, with the strongest regression and crash guardrails"; growth, "maximize installs, return visits and revenue within the trust rules". The judges were a Korean mobile market veteran who had shipped top-10 utility apps, a staff Android engineer responsible for crash-free rate and APK size on low-end Samsung phones, and a Google Play and AdMob policy and privacy reviewer. The script picked the winner by the sum of the three judges' totals. A majority vote would also have chosen quality, the pick of judges 2 and 3; with only the speed design on the table, the NoDisplay entry would have gone straight to implementation.

The speed design's entry point: async copy in a NoDisplay activity

The speed design planned nine milestones totalling 20.5 days. All document intents went to one EntryActivity with Theme.NoDisplay. On Dispatchers.IO it would take the URI, sniff the format from the first 64 KB, copy the file into app storage while hashing it with SHA-256, start the reader and finish, showing progress and a cancel button after one second.

A NoDisplay activity has to call finish() before onResume() completes. For apps targeting API 23 or higher on Android 6.0 or later, one that does not crashes with IllegalStateException and the message "did not call finish() prior to onResume() completing". A CommonsWare blog post flagged it in November 2015 and noted that activities doing their work in onCreate() and finishing right there seem to be fine. Our app targets API 36, and an async copy finishes after onResume(), so as designed, every "open with" from KakaoTalk would have crashed the app.

At design time there was no code to run. Written as designed, it would compile; it shows up only in a test that runs the activity lifecycle, such as Robolectric, or when a device opens a file through a VIEW intent. Judge 2 called it easy to fix but fatal if built as written. Judge 3 said to switch to Theme.Translucent.NoTitleBar.

The final plan has the reader activity take VIEW intents directly, and a Translucent SendEntryActivity hand shared files on and finish inside onCreate(). The architecture document lists the NoDisplay entry as a rejected option, and the PRD acceptance criteria include "zero Theme.NoDisplay activities".

Judge 1 picked the design with the crash

JudgespeedqualitygrowthPick
1 market veteran343332speed
2 Android engineer293534quality
3 policy and privacy reviewer323632quality
Total9510498quality

Judge 1 listed ten fatal flaws, none of them NoDisplay. The three judges gave speed 8, 7 and 8 for win potential. Quality got 9 for reliability from all three, but its milestones added up to 44 days, and all three said it would miss the October demand window. Growth (39 days) contradicted itself: one quality gate required switching to a preview within 6 seconds while its state machine showed a notice at 8 seconds and terminated at 30.

Judge 3 also caught that the app lock in the speed and growth designs used BIOMETRIC_STRONG|DEVICE_CREDENTIAL, which API 28 and 29 do not support. With minSdk 29, that paid feature would not have worked on Android 10 phones. The judges' 25 fatal flaws were merged into nine rows in the analysis document, each with its fix.

23 gaps in the merged plan: a schedule that did not add up and a gate that could not run

The synthesis agent started from the quality design, grafted in the speed design's scope cuts and parallel work, and fixed every fatal flaw. The critic's checklist found 2 blockers, 10 major and 11 minor gaps in the result.

Blocker 1 was arithmetic: the milestones on the critical path summed to 23 working days, so even with no weekends the internal-track date was already missed. Blocker 2 was a release gate that could not run. It required a shell script to pass on a Firebase Test Lab device, and Test Lab gives you no adb shell. The gate was split in two, and the first build milestone (M1) got a spike for instrumented tests on a release build.

One major gap concerned password-protected files. For a fast first screen, the plan showed the preview image stored inside the HWP file before rendering, and a research-stage experiment had found that image in encrypted documents too, so the first page would show before the password. It became one functional requirement and one architecture section. The analysis document has a table mapping each of the 23 gaps to where it was fixed.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The NoDisplay entry never reached git, and the ban test closed two bypasses

Early on October 5 the first implementation workflow (M1 and M2) added a NoDisplay ban to an architecture test. A review agent in the same workflow found two ways around it: the <application> theme, which activities inherit, and a style item android:windowNoDisplay=true. The test, which never launches an activity, now reads every themed element in the manifest plus style parents and that item, and each bypass was planted once to confirm the test fails.

Only one commit in the history contains the word NoDisplay: the October 8 internal test build, which brought in the ban test and the design documents. On October 9 the owner sent HWPX, HWP5, PDF and HWP3 files from another KakaoTalk account to a Galaxy S23 and all four opened.

The NoDisplay entry was first proposed by a refuting reviewer

The intents research report never mentioned NoDisplay. The entry came from the fact-checking reviewer of that report, as its suggested replacement: "VIEW and SEND are received by a very light trampoline (Theme.NoDisplay, excludeFromRecents, noHistory)", with the trampoline starting the 64 KB sniff and the copy. That text went into the dossier and the speed design followed it. The quality and growth designs did not use the NoDisplay theme.

Judge 3 tagged the NoDisplay flaw "[verified, Android 6.0 behavior change]", but that agent made one tool call, the one that submitted its result, so the tag was added without opening anything. The claim was right; we confirmed it against the CommonsWare post while writing this. The three design agents and judge 3 worked only from the dossier pasted into the prompt; judges 1 and 2 looked at the git history and spike files once or twice.

The schedule estimate was wrong in the other direction. The analysis said the original November 3 production date could not be met and set the internal track for November 2, production for November 9 and November 13 to 16 as the worst case. The internal track came on October 8 and the public release on October 10. Some milestone exit criteria, such as purchase restore, the app lock on API 29 and TalkBack checks on a device, were still open at release. We had told the critic to judge estimates for one developer plus Claude; the build then ran as separate workflows, one or two milestones each.

The document-writing agent was assigned five files and wrote four. The agent's permission settings blocked it from writing the analysis report as a file; it did not work around the block and returned the text in its answer, which the main session saved; the workflow record lists all 45 agents as done.

How to run it: the script skeleton and the order

A trimmed skeleton of the real script: prompt text removed, and helper names such as dropRefuted, argmax and sumTotals are illustrative (the original does this inline). agent, parallel and pipeline come from Claude Code Workflow scripts.

const verified = await pipeline(AREAS,
  a => agent(CTX + a.task, { schema: REPORT }),
  (r, a) => parallel(['fact-check', a.lens].map(l => () =>
    agent(CTX + LENS[l] + JSON.stringify(r), { schema: VERDICT }))))
const dossier = dropRefuted(verified)          // 16 findings removed
const designs = await parallel(ANGLES.map(an => () =>
  agent(CTX + an.priority + dossier, { schema: DESIGN })))
const judged = await parallel(JUDGES.map(j => () =>
  agent(CTX + j + designs + dossier, { schema: SCORE })))
const winner = argmax(sumTotals(judged))       // sum, not one judge
const final = await agent(CTX + winner + designs + judged + dossier, { schema: DESIGN })
const gaps = await agent(CTX + CHECKLIST + final + dossier, { schema: CRIT })
  1. Give every research area one fact-checking reviewer and one reviewer with an area lens, and drop refuted findings before design.
  2. Have every design use the same dossier and the same schema, changing only the priority sentence. Put day estimates in the schema so schedules can be compared.
  3. Use three judges from different angles, such as market, engineering and policy, and decide by the total. Ask for fatal flaws and graft ideas separately.
  4. Run a checklist critique on the final plan, and keep a table of where each gap was fixed.
  5. Pin each fatal flaw with a rule test, such as an architecture test that parses the manifest and styles, and remove the guard once to see the test fail.
  6. Keep checks only a person can do, like opening files on a real phone, on a separate list and close them there.

Review after the code exists is a different process; we ran one where every finding faces three refuting agents, described in AI code review findings: fix only what survives refutation.

When 8.8 million tokens and an hour are wasted

Verification used the most tokens, 2.95 million. The nine design, judge and synthesis agents made 21 tool calls between them and used 3.84 million tokens, because each prompt carried the whole dossier as JSON. We did not record a dollar cost.

If the design has nothing to argue about, say one more screen or a feature whose API is already chosen, this is too much. Here a new app, two rendering engines, the entry path, monetization and Play policy were all in play at once. Every agent was the same model reading the same dossier, so a flaw they all miss stays missed, and the scores are not calibrated: the same speed design got anywhere from 29 to 34.

What to check next

As of the October 9 record, opening files received through Naver Mail (a major Korean email service) and Gmail had not been tested on a device.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Building the SugarDoc HWP viewer: all 8 parts

  1. Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents

FAQ

Is one judge enough?

Not in this run. With only the market-veteran judge, the speed design with the NoDisplay crash would have won with 34 points. The Android engineer and policy reviewer personas caught the crash.

Why does a Theme.NoDisplay activity crash?

For apps targeting API 23 or higher on Android 6.0 or later, a NoDisplay activity that has not called finish() by the end of onResume() throws IllegalStateException. If the work is asynchronous, use a Translucent theme or receive the intent in a real screen.

Sources: git history and design documents in the SugarDoc repository and the Claude Code session logs (workflow script, per-agent transcripts), as of October 26, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We set interstitial frequency from device timelines, and tutorials don't count
  • We built three photo apps before checking the market: this year's new apps had a median of 1,166 installs
