item.title: A permission table for a scheduled AI agent – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

A permission table for a scheduled AI agent: what it does alone, and which clicks a person makes

We split the agent's work into three lanes in one file: what it does alone, what it does after approval, and the clicks a person makes even after approving. Every scheduled run reads that file first.

Giving an agent rules and limits 4/5

An AI coding agent such as Claude Code can rerun the same prompt at set times. Those runs happen while nobody is watching, so rules given in chat never reach them; only a file the run reads does. Since October 17, 2026, SugarMount has had the agent market Arrow Knots and Block Turn this way, four times a day, with the final click on money, accounts and policy left to a person. Even an ad restart the operator had approved was blocked by the tool's permission check, and a person switched it on.

The table started with three columns and a list of stop conditions

The schedule is one morning market check and three work blocks a day. The first sentence of the work-block prompt says to read the operating rules file first; the rest says to pick the most urgent item from the to-do list, work on it within the permissions, and update the posting log and the day's report. The permission table is one section of that rules file.

The first column is what the agent may do alone: measurement, analysis, drafts, posting from accounts that already exist, and replying to comments on its own posts. Posting comes with numbers: at most two promotional posts a day, at least three days between posts on the same site, and always say you are the developer. The second column needs the operator's approval: anything that costs money (restarting ads, budget or bid changes, paid services), new sign-ups, logins and CAPTCHAs, policy declarations, and entering a real name or contact details. The third column is what the agent never does: fake accounts, rating manipulation, channels whose cost or eligibility is unchecked, and channels the operator has closed.

Below the table sit five stop conditions, copied as they are into the template further down. When one applies, the agent does not act. It marks the item Blocked and writes the options and a recommendation at the top of the daily report under "needs your decision". The numeric limits worked too: on October 18 the posting log shows "two promotional posts today, limit reached" after the second post, and nothing else went up that day.

Rules given in chat never reached the scheduled runs

It started on the evening of October 8. The operator told the agent to do all of it, and the agent replied that it would begin by creating an ads account and linking Google Play. Five minutes later the operator said: anything that spends money or looks odd, ask first. That one line was the first rule.

It only caught the moment of payment, and the trouble up to October 10 involved no money at all. Reddit had removed all our posts, and on the 10th a Korean community board suspended the account on its first post, as advertising. We traced it to new accounts dropping the same link in several places at once, and set the two-a-day and three-day limits. On October 13 the agent pushed ahead with the Galaxy Store without confirming cost or eligibility; only after two release builds were ready did the portal say Android apps need a paid seller account, and the channel was dropped. So the trigger changed from "payment" to categories, and those became the five stop conditions.

Where a rule lives mattered too. The October 8 rule sat only in the memory of a different working folder, so the marketing session never loaded it (what a long session reloads is in What survives Claude Code auto-compaction: the summary, recent files and the memory index). The only place a rule reliably reaches every run is a file the prompt names. It is the same idea as How to write AGENTS.md: only the rules an AI coding agent gets wrong, except that this table governs work outside the repository.

A tool permission check sits between approval and the click

Claude Code's auto mode asks a permission classifier before it runs a click or a command. In the marketing session the classifier refused 11 actions between October 17 and 20.

The most common reason covered making a Short public, uploading a promo image and saving a store listing. The refusals with no reason hit submitting listing changes for review and a publish step, and the shared-resources refusal stopped a command that would have changed a setting on every connected test phone.

On the afternoon of October 18 the operator said to finish everything, yet the custom store listing's submit and save buttons were refused, and they only passed after the operator asked for the save again. At 17:06 the operator approved the rest of the batch, and a minute later the click on the ad status menu came back with Permission for this action was denied by the Claude Code auto mode classifier. Reason: [Real-World Transactions]. Fourteen seconds later the same reason blocked an emulator boot check that had nothing to do with ads. In the end the operator switched the ad on.

So the approval column really splits in two: work the agent finishes once approved, and clicks a person makes even after approving. Between October 17 and 22 the posting log has seven lines where a permission check pushed the final step to a person. On October 22 an update post on a Korean gaming community sat fully filled in while the operator pressed only the submit button. Do not have the agent hunt for a workaround on a click that spends money, even after approval. Put it in the person's lane from the start, and have the agent say so the moment it is blocked.

Where the agent got it wrong: a report 3 hours 38 minutes late, and log times that were off

The ad click was blocked at 17:07, but the agent told the operator it needed a person at 20:45. In between it said nothing about the block and moved on to the rest of the approved batch, an emulator test, where one connection check waited more than three hours for a reply. That ran against the memory rule it had written 26 minutes earlier: when a check blocks you, do not leave the tab open and move on, ask right away. Now a refused click marks only that item Blocked, and it shows up at the top of that day's report under "needs your decision".

The log times were wrong as well. The posting log records the episode as "18:40 restart attempted, on hold" and "20:00 switched on, running"; the transcript says blocked at 17:07 and reported at 20:45. The agent wrote both lines later, from memory. On October 20 it logged an Instagram share as on hold after the share button was refused; the next day the post turned out to be live already.

It also erred in the timid direction. In the October 18 performance report the agent proposed posting to the community boards only at updates, where views sat around 100 to 200, and dropping one channel if its next video also got zero views. The operator corrected it: free channels grow by steady accumulation. Its memory now says: never propose cutting a channel; when results are weak, propose a different format.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

What we dropped, and what we did not use

Asking before every action never fit. The runs happen while nobody is watching, and even now one release approval and one ad decision sat at the top of the daily report for four days. Leaving it all to the tool's permission check failed too: the classifier knows nothing of two posts a day, three days per site or closed channels, it blocked posts the table allows, and 3 of its 11 refusals came with no reason.

Claude Code has its own permission controls: allow and deny rules in settings.json, and hooks that run a script just before a tool call. The user settings for these runs had neither (checked October 23). Those rules match tool names and command patterns. Marketing work is mostly browser clicks, so a click on a publish button looks like any other click to them, and counting two posts a day would need a hook that keeps its own state. Work that a command pattern can catch, such as a release script, is held more firmly by a deny rule than by a document.

Running the agent from an OS scheduler outside the session is the other option. There is no session end and no seven-day expiry, so no runs get lost. The cost is the hand-off: the agent leaves a filled-in browser tab and a person presses the last button, and that flow has to be built separately. This time we used session jobs and kept the expiry date in the table so they get registered again.

When this does not fit

The biggest limit is that the schedule lives inside the session. The registration output read "Session-only (not written to disk, dies when Claude exits). Auto-expires after 7 days." On October 22 the session ended during a move to a new development setup, and the morning check and the morning work block were skipped. If a job must never miss a day, use a scheduler outside the session.

It also fails if nobody reads the daily report. Pending decisions pile up and the important work stops first. The two-a-day and three-day numbers were set for a few Korean gaming boards; other channels need numbers from their own rules. Work full of logins, CAPTCHAs and locked phones stays largely manual whatever the table says.

How to set it up: a permission table template

This skeleton takes the three columns above and splits approval in two, giving four lanes. Copy it into a file and name that file in the first sentence of every scheduled prompt. Write the date of the incident behind each row; later, that date tells you whether the row can go.

# Permission table (every scheduled run reads this file first and follows it)
Schedule expires: YYYY-MM-DD / register again on: YYYY-MM-DD
## 1. Agent alone
- (task) | limit: _ a day, _ days apart per site | added: YYYY-MM-DD
## 2. Agent after approval
- (task) | added:
## 3. A person clicks, even after approving
- status changes that spend money
- final clicks a permission check refused (fill everything in, leave the tab open)
## 4. Never
- (task) | added:
## Stop and ask (if any applies, do not act)
- a kind of work done for the first time
- work on weak evidence
- anything publicly visible
- anything hard to undo
- anything touching money, accounts or policy
-> mark Blocked; options and a recommendation at the top of the report
## When blocked
- login, CAPTCHA or permission denial: Blocked for that item only, move on
- write a permission denial at the top of this run's report
- two failures in a row on one item: stop, "needs your action"
## Logs
- copy times from tool output, not from memory

Our values: lane 1 is two posts a day and three days per site, lane 3 holds ad status changes and publish clicks a permission check refused, and lane 4 holds proposals to cut channels.

What is left

Session jobs have to be registered again every seven days. The next number to count is how many days a "needs your decision" item waits before it is decided; the log already has a four-day case. If that number does not drop, the fix is to change when the report gets read, not to shrink the person's lane.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Giving an agent rules and limits: all 5 parts

  1. What survives Claude Code auto-compaction: the summary, recent files and the memory index
  2. Keeping secrets away from an AI coding agent: one rule for chat, logs and token permissions

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Claude Code scheduled job last?

The session jobs used here expire after seven days and stop as soon as the session ends, so the rules file carries a renewal date and the jobs are registered again before they lapse.

Why is the agent's click blocked after a person approved it?

The tool's permission classifier judges each click on its own, apart from any approval in the chat. That is why clicks that spend money sit in the person's lane from the start.

What should an AI agent ask about before acting?

Five things: a channel tried for the first time, work on weak evidence, anything publicly visible, anything hard to undo, and anything touching money, accounts or policy. "Anything that costs money" alone was not enough, because in one case the cost only showed up at the last step.

Sources: the operating rules file and posting log (October 9 to 22, 2026), daily reports, agent memory files and the Claude Code session transcript. Times are Korea Standard Time.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Android blank Hangul: 8,693 empty glyphs in cmap – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Android showed some Hangul as blank gaps: NanumSquare's cmap claimed 11,172 syllables but drew only 2,479

When a font's cmap says it has a character it cannot draw, Android uses that font anyway and paints a blank instead of falling back to the system font. Removing the empty entries from the cmap fixed it.

On the night of 2026-09-15, the operator of our Korean spelling checker, SugarSpeller, noticed that the rare syllable 밣 showed up in the input box but turned into an empty gap inside the chat bubble. The cause was the bundled NanumSquare Light font. Its cmap (the table that maps character codes to glyph numbers) listed all 11,172 precomposed Hangul syllables, yet 8,693 of those glyphs had zero bytes of outline data. We removed 13,948 outline-less entries from the cmap, and the fix shipped in version 1.6.017.

Sources: the fix commit, the 1.6.017 changelog entry and the work log in the app repository. Numbers were re-measured on 2026-10-22 from the font files before and after the fix.

The glyph for 밣 had 0 bytes and a width of 910

Android's text layout engine, Minikin, picks the font for each character by reading the cmap. It never checks whether the outline is empty. Following 밣 (U+BC23) through the file gives a four-step chain.

  1. The cmap maps U+BC23 to glyph 12552.
  2. The loca table (where each glyph's data starts and ends) gives glyph 12552 a length of 0.
  3. The hmtx table still gives it an advance width of 910, the same as a normal syllable such as 받. So the reader sees a one-character gap, not a tofu box. All 8,693 empty syllables had width 910.
  4. Since the app font already answered yes, no fallback to the system font happens.

Once the entry is out of the cmap, the app font says no and Android finds the character in the system font. The cmap went from 17,559 entries to 3,611.

Re-measured: only 2,479 syllables had outlines

These values come from reading the tables directly with Python's struct module, without fontTools.

ItemBeforeAfter
Hangul syllables in the cmap11,1722,479
Of those, 0-byte outlines8,6930
Visible characters with no outline (spaces and controls excluded)13,9480
Characters with outlines3,5753,575
Glyph count18,15518,155
File size (bytes)750,932715,448

The 13,948 split into 8,693 Hangul syllables, 4,890 Han characters (hanja) and 365 others, including the bullet • and several arrows. Not a single hanja could be drawn by this font. The 2,479 surviving syllables are all 2,350 syllables of KS X 1001, the legacy Korean character set that covers everyday text, plus 129 more. Those 129 include 뷁, which is outside KS X 1001. A test that used 뷁 as its "rare syllable" would have passed.

Only the chat bubble broke because it was a TextView

The symptom as first described: visible in the input box, blank in the bubble, fine on the Classic screen. The app theme applied this font to every TextView through android:textViewStyle, and the bubble was a TextView. The input box and the Classic result box were EditTexts. According to the commit, AppCompat's EditText does not pick up the theme's android:editTextStyle, so they used the system font. The Classic screen survived by accident. Every TextView in the app was affected.

The agent's first check said 밣 was there

An AI coding agent found the cause, but its first measurement pointed the wrong way. It only checked whether 밣 was in each font's cmap: NanumSquare said yes, and the Gamja Flower subset used for greeting cards said no. What turned it around was file size. A font with 17,559 cmap entries in 750 KB looked too small to hold every syllable, so the agent measured outline lengths. The 8,693 figure came out 1 minute 35 seconds after the problem was raised.

The first trial fix was wrong too. It removed 13,991 entries without filtering, including 32 control characters and 3 space characters that are supposed to be empty. Right after the operator approved the plan, the agent re-filtered by Unicode category before applying it, and the final count became 13,948.

The third mistake was caught by a person. After committing, the agent said it could not check rendering on a device and handed the visual check to the operator, even though it had booted an Android 14 emulator in software mode the day before in the same session. The operator asked for a deep review and cross-check before release, and granted the KVM permission the agent asked for. At 08:37 the next morning, an Android 14 emulator showed both 밣받다 and • fully drawn.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The font was probably shipped this way

The commit message guessed that "a subsetting tool removed the glyphs but kept the cmap". While writing this note we ran the same measurement on the NanumSquare files the site uses to draw figures. NanumSquare ExtraBold matched the app's file exactly: 8,693 empty syllables, 13,948 visible characters without outlines. NanumSquare Regular had 8,822 empty syllables (Figure 2).

The site's files are weights the app never had, so they are not copies. All three carry a 2016 "Version 1.000" build string, and the app's file was already in the repository's first commit on 2020-12-16. We have not compared them with the official download, so the commit's guess stays unconfirmed. For contrast, the properly cut Gamja Flower subset listed only 2,349 syllables in its cmap.

We trimmed the cmap instead of swapping fonts or adding a fallback chain

NanumGothic, already in the app at 4,691,820 bytes, draws all 11,172 syllables, but switching to it changes the look of the whole app. Replacing the file with a complete NanumSquare Light was estimated at about 4 MB more, and the measurements above make it unclear whether such a file exists. Outside the session we also considered a fallback chain with Typeface.CustomFallbackBuilder (API 29). It does not help, because the font for each character is still chosen by cmap.

Trimming the cmap keeps every glyph in place, so the result can be checked one to one against the original. The cost is that rare syllables and hanja appear in the system typeface. If you bundle a font in a Korean app, do not trust cmap coverage to tell you it "supports Hangul". Add a test that measures outline lengths.

When this check does not work

  • CFF-based OTF fonts have no loca table. The app's regression test treats the length as -1 there and passes silently.
  • Fonts with only a format 12 cmap: the test reads format 4 only and passes on an empty map.
  • Characters the system font also lacks still show tofu after the trim.
  • Screens where every character must share one typeface need a different font.

We checked View-based TextViews on one Android 14 emulator. We did not check Compose Text.

How to check the fonts in your own app

  1. List every font in res/font and assets.
  2. For each font, read glyph numbers from the cmap and lengths from loca, and count entries with length 0. Skip Unicode categories Cc, Cf, Zs, Zl, Zp and the three Hangul fillers (U+115F, U+1160, U+3164).
  3. Compare the number of drawable syllables with the 2,350 of KS X 1001.
  4. Pick on-screen test characters from the step 2 output.

Step 2 takes the 24 lines below. On the original file it prints blank 13948 / hangul 11172, drawn 2479. On a CFF-based OTF font it stops with KeyError: 'loca', because there is no loca table, and on a font without a format 4 subtable it prints hangul 0 (checked on 2026-10-23 with Noto Sans KR OTF and with a copy whose format 4 subtables were relabeled). If you see hangul 0, check the subtable formats first.

import struct, sys, unicodedata
d = open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read()
u16 = lambda p: struct.unpack_from(">H", d, p)[0]
u32 = lambda p: struct.unpack_from(">I", d, p)[0]
T = {d[12+16*i:16+16*i].decode("latin1"): u32(20+16*i) for i in range(u16(4))}
def glyph_len(g):                      # loca: short(0) / long(1)
    lo = T["loca"]
    if u16(T["head"] + 50): return u32(lo+4*g+4) - u32(lo+4*g)
    return 2 * (u16(lo+2*g+2) - u16(lo+2*g))
cmap = {}
for i in range(u16(T["cmap"] + 2)):    # format 4 subtables only
    s = T["cmap"] + u32(T["cmap"] + 8 + 8*i)
    if u16(s) != 4: continue
    n = u16(s + 6); e = s + 14; st = e + n + 2; de = st + n; ro = de + n
    for k in range(0, n, 2):
        a, b, dl, r = u16(st+k), u16(e+k), struct.unpack_from(">h", d, de+k)[0], u16(ro+k)
        for c in range(a, min(b, 0xFFFE) + 1):
            g = (c + dl) & 0xFFFF if r == 0 else u16(ro + k + r + 2*(c - a))
            if r and g: g = (g + dl) & 0xFFFF
            if g: cmap[c] = g
ok = lambda c: c in (0x115F, 0x1160, 0x3164) or unicodedata.category(chr(c)) in ("Cc", "Cf", "Zs", "Zl", "Zp")
blank = [c for c, g in cmap.items() if glyph_len(g) == 0 and not ok(c)]
han = [c for c in cmap if 0xAC00 <= c <= 0xD7A3]
print(f"blank {len(blank)} / hangul {len(han)}, drawn {sum(glyph_len(cmap[c]) > 0 for c in han)}")

The cleanup itself was a fontTools script added in the fix commit. With fontTools it deletes, in every cmap subtable, the entries that point to outline-less glyphs, and keeps the characters skipped in step 2. It refuses fonts without a glyf table.

font = TTFont(src)
glyf = font["glyf"]
for table in font["cmap"].tables:
    cmap = getattr(table, "cmap", None) or {}
    for cp, name in list(cmap.items()):
        if glyf[name].numberOfContours == 0 and not is_blank_ok(cp):
            del cmap[cp]
font.save(dst)
  1. After trimming, confirm every removed entry was empty and the count of characters with outlines is unchanged (3,575 here).
  2. Put the original font back and make sure the test fails, as in Catch fake AI-written tests by deleting their guards.
  3. Check that base/res/font in the release AAB holds the fixed file.

What is left

The site's figure and share-image tools use those same NanumSquare files, so any syllable outside KS X 1001 would come out blank in a figure (the second cell of the first figure), so this note keeps 밣 out of its title. Swapping the figure font and teaching the app's test about CFF and format 12 are still open.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why do some Korean characters show as blank spaces in my Android app?

Most likely your bundled font lists them in its cmap but has empty outlines for them. Measuring the outline length behind each cmap entry shows it at once.

How do I tell a tofu box (□) from a blank gap?

A tofu box means no font, fallbacks included, has the character. A gap one character wide means the cmap lists it but the outline is empty. Every empty syllable in this font had width 910.

Which characters should I use to test a Korean font?

Ones the font actually cannot draw, found by inspecting it. This font drew 뷁 but not 밣.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Korean line breaks in Compose and stacked labels – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

Jetpack Compose splits Korean between syllables, but the stacked 'R/u/l/e' label came from how a Row measures

Jetpack Compose breaks Korean words between syllables. A shared WordBreak.Phrase style and a longest-word width check fixed it; the vertically stacked labels had a separate cause.

In a row that puts a label next to its value, the word "Rule" was standing on its end: R, u, l, e, one letter per line. We saw it on September 25, 2026, during a real-device pass of three photo apps on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15), and the same shape turned up in "Versio/n", "1.0.1-debu/g" and the Korean "오른쪽으/로" ("to the right", split before its last syllable). They looked alike but had two causes. The first three came from a Row that measured the value first and left the label almost no width. The Korean one came from Compose treating every Hangul syllable boundary as a break point. Both were fixed, separately, in one design-system module the three apps share.

Sources: the fix commit and same-day changelog in the app repository, the HWP Viewer SugarDoc device test report (2026-10-06) and the Android Developers reference, as of October 21, 2026.

Five broken spots, all inside shared components

Every defect sat in a shared component. The September 25 QA was run by four AI coding agents in turn: one per app, then a fourth that reproduced every finding with its own screenshots and read the code behind each root cause. The table copies the symptoms recorded that day in the CHANGELOG and in code comments.

SymptomComponentCauseFix
"R/u/l/e", "Versio/n", "1.0.1-debu/g"Label/value rows, settings rowsRow measured the value first and gave the label what was leftPairLayout: side by side if both fit, otherwise the value drops below
"오른쪽으/로", "Transparen/t PNG"Option tile grid, action buttonsA word wider than its cell; Compose reported one Hangul syllable as the minimum widthMeasure the longest word and fall back to one column
"Quick compress" did not fit a third of the widthSegmented controlLarge fontStacked tiles from 150% font scale
"Web" and "Custom" hidden off-screenChoice chip rowHorizontal scrollingFlowRow wrapping
Korean words such as "메일" (mail) could split at 200% fontEvery text styleSyllable boundaries counted as break pointsWordBreak.Phrase

The three apps are Compress Image, Flip & Rotate Image and Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP, and all of them depend on the same design-system module. The fix commit touched 57 files, but the line-breaking work is concentrated in a handful of files in that module.

Compose treats Hangul syllable boundaries as break points

LineBreak.WordBreak decides where Compose may split a word. The LineBreak.WordBreak reference describes Default as the locale's default word-breaking rules: Latin scripts break between words, while languages that don't use whitespace (the page's example is Japanese) can break between characters. Phrase does not insert breaks between characters of the same phrase unit and is "ideal for short text such as titles and UI labels". Both values were added in Compose 1.3.0.

Korean does put spaces between words, yet the apps still split inside them. A comment in the repository's WordWidth.kt records why: Compose's own minimum intrinsic width treats every Hangul syllable as a break point. So the grid believed "오른쪽으로" fitted in the width of a single syllable, kept two columns and cut the word in the middle.

The platform adds its own limit. Per the LineBreakConfig reference, phrase-based breaking (LINE_BREAK_WORD_STYLE_PHRASE) arrived in API level 33 (Android 13), its support depends on the locale, and it has no effect where the locale is unsupported. These apps have minSdk 29, which means Phrase does nothing on Android 10 to 12.

WordBreak.Phrase lives in one shared TextStyle

A single style() function in SugarType.kt builds every step of the type scale, so it is the only place that sets lineBreak. No screen code changed.

private val WordAwareBreak =
    LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase)
private fun style(weight: FontWeight, size: Int, line: Int, spacing: Boolean = false) = TextStyle(
    // fontFamily, fontSize, lineHeight, letterSpacing ...
    lineBreak = WordAwareBreak,
)

If your Compose app has Korean screens, set Phrase once in the shared TextStyle and do not add it to individual Text calls. Per-screen settings get forgotten the next time someone adds a screen. The same comment says a word wider than the line still breaks. (The Korean hero titles also got zero-width break points after the "·" separator.)

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The longest word decides how many columns fit

The option tile grid picks its column count from the minimum intrinsic width each tile reports. For Korean that number is one syllable wide, so the module gained a function that measures whole words: split on whitespace, measure each word on one line, return the widest.

text.split(Regex("\\s+")).filter { it.isNotEmpty() }.maxOfOrNull { word ->
    measurer.measure(word, style, softWrap = false, maxLines = 1).size.width
} ?: 0

Tile titles and subtitles report that value as their minimum intrinsic width (minIntrinsicWidthAtLeast, a small LayoutModifier), and the grid compares it with the cell width.

val cols = when {
    requested == 1 -> 1
    largeFont -> 1
    measurables.any { it.minIntrinsicWidth(Constraints.Infinity) > cellWidthFor(requested) } -> 1
    else -> requested
}

In app code, Flip & Rotate Image's four action buttons use the same function. When the longest word of any label is wider than half the screen minus the button chrome, the buttons go one per row instead of two.

From 150% font scale, stack; for chips, use FlowRow

One constant defines "large font": LARGE_FONT_SCALE = 1.5f in Chips.kt. At or above it, three components switch to a vertical layout.

  • Segmented control: the segments become option tiles stacked top to bottom. The check icon went too; it was taking a third of a segment's width.
  • Option tile grid: one column, whatever was requested.
  • Flip & Rotate Image's action buttons: one per row.

The choice chip row used to be a Row with horizontalScroll. Chips past the edge simply hid there, and nothing told the user that "Web" or "Custom" existed. With FlowRow they wrap onto the next line.

// before: Row(modifier = modifier.horizontalScroll(rememberScrollState()), ...)
FlowRow(
    modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(SugarSpacing.sm),
) { /* FilterChip ... */ }

A Row from four days earlier, and a button width that missed by 2 px

"R/u/l/e" had nothing to do with Korean. The label/value row came from the design v2 commit (2026-09-21), written together with an AI coding agent. It was a Row with Modifier.weight(1f, fill = false) on the label and no weight on the value. A Row measures unweighted children first, so a long value took the whole width and the label folded into the few pixels left, one letter per line.

Four days later, the cross-check agent in the device QA flagged this structure while reading the code behind the finding. The new PairLayout measures each slot's natural width (maxIntrinsicWidth) first. If the sum fits the line, they sit side by side; if not, the value moves under the label.

The second mistake was a number. The action-button chrome adds up to exactly 76 dp: 24 dp of OutlinedButton padding on each side, a 20 dp icon and an 8 dp gap. According to the code comment, at 130% font "오른쪽으로" measured 2 px under the space that exact figure left, and it still wrapped. The value was fixed at BUTTON_CHROME = 84.dp, the exact chrome plus 8 dp of slack.

The same defect came back by another route. In the HWP Viewer SugarDoc device test on 2026-10-06, the format placeholder split into "HW/PX" (S21) and "HW/P" (S20) at 200% font. That app uses the same design-system module, so Phrase was already on, but "HWPX" is a single word and a word wider than its box still breaks. Pinning the placeholder to one line and letting it shrink to fit fixed that, but "HWP 3.0" did not fit even at the smallest step and got clipped to "HWP 3.(" instead. The final fix shortened placeholder names to four characters or fewer ("HWP3"), while the badge and the TalkBack label keep "HWP 3.0".

Checklist

After the September 25 fixes, a separate agent checked every fix on the device and a person checked again by hand, across 1.0/1.3/2.0 font scale, Korean and English, light and dark, and landscape, with no regressions. The list below is drawn from these fixes.

  • The shared TextStyle sets lineBreak = LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase). Android 12 and lower ignore it, so the items below still matter.
  • Layouts that choose a column count look at the longest word, not Compose's minimum intrinsic width.
  • At fontScale 1.5 and above, segmented controls, grids and button rows switch to a vertical layout.
  • No option hides behind horizontal scrolling (FlowRow).
  • Label/value rows are not left to Row weights.
  • Computed padding includes the error seen on a device (8 dp this time).
  • Single-word short labels, such as format names like "HWPX", fit their box at 200% font.

One item is still open: on the input screen of Convert Image JPG PNG WEBP, the size badge wraps as "JPEG · 1.3 / MB", recorded as a cosmetic leftover in the 2026-09-25 CHANGELOG entry. The full pre-release check list is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

How do I make Jetpack Compose wrap Korean by word instead of by syllable?

Set lineBreak = LineBreak.Simple.copy(wordBreak = LineBreak.WordBreak.Phrase) in your TextStyle. Put it in the shared typography once and every Text picks it up. Android 12 and lower ignore it, so keep a layout check based on the longest word as well.

Why does a word still split in the middle with WordBreak.Phrase?

Phrase still breaks a word that is wider than its line or cell. Widen the cell, use fewer columns or shorten the text. HWP Viewer SugarDoc saw the 'HWPX' placeholder split into 'HW/PX' at 200% font, pinned it to one line with auto-shrink, and shortened 'HWP 3.0', which still did not fit, to 'HWP3'.

Which font scales should a Compose layout be tested at?

These apps were checked at 1.0, 1.3 and 2.0 font scale, combined with Korean and English, light and dark, and landscape. Their layouts switch to vertical at 1.5, so test on both sides of that switch.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Fitting a JPEG under a file size limit: quality binary search, a predicted long edge, and a final check against the original
  • The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

item.title: Play staged rollout API: 20% went out as 100% – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

A 20% staged rollout went out at 100%: a completed release in the Play Publisher API cannot go back to staged

Drop the fraction from a staged rollout through the Play Publisher API and the release is committed as completed, with no way back to 20%. Read back status and userFraction before you commit.

Reworking a long-running spelling app 6/8

A staged rollout on Google Play sends a new version to part of your users, say 20%, and widens it once nothing breaks. We let an agent run releases through the Publisher API, and on October 11, 2026 a command meant to ship SugarSpeller 1.6.029 to 20% committed it to everyone, because of one argument-count check in its script. Thirty-five seconds later, a request to set it back came back HTTP 403. Below: the terminal output from that day, why Play refused, the promotion script we use now, and one check that is still missing from it.

The command got 0.2 and sent completed

The agent ran play3.py promote 97 "97 (1.6.029)" notes29.json production 0.2. The trailing 0.2 was the rollout fraction. This is how the script picked it up:

a=sys.argv; FR=None
if a[1] in ("upload","promote") and len(a)>(8 if a[1]=="upload" else 7): FR=a.pop()
...
**({"status":"inProgress","userFraction":float(FR)} if FR else {"status":"completed"})

That command produces seven entries in sys.argv, counting the script name. The check wanted more than seven before it would take the fraction. Off by one, FR stayed empty, and the default for "no fraction" was completed. The upload branch was off by one the same way.

The script was never in the repository. The agent had made it earlier in the same session by patching an older script with sed, and since the internal-track upload passed no fraction, nothing had exposed the bug. (vc97 was itself a same-day rebuild. A deep check on a Galaxy S21 that afternoon found an old bug where launching with the screen off left the app stuck on a black splash, so vc96 was dropped and the fix went into a new build.)

The PUT back to 20% got 403 PERMISSION_DENIED

The agent opened a new edit straight away and tried to set the production track to "vc97 inProgress 0.2, previous vc94 completed". Play answered:

before [('97 (1.6.029)', 'completed', ['97'], None)]
put [('97 (1.6.029)', 'inProgress', 0.2), ('94 (1.6.027)', 'completed', None)]
HTTP 403 {
  "error": {
    "code": 403,
    "message": "You cannot rollout this release because it does not allow any existing users to upgrade to the newly added APKs.",
    "status": "PERMISSION_DENIED"
  }
}

The edits.tracks reference defines completed as a release that "will have no further changes" and is served to all users. userFraction can only be set when the status is inProgress or halted, and must sit between 0 and 1. Nothing in the docs describes putting a fraction back on a release that has already gone to everyone, and we found no paragraph explaining this particular 403 message.

The agent printed completed and committed anyway

There were two mistakes, and the second was bigger than the off-by-one above. The script printed the track from the PUT response as track production [('97 (1.6.029)', 'completed')] and went on to commit in the same run without checking it.

Afterwards the agent tried to fix the check with sed, and Claude Code's automatic permission check blocked the edit. The agent told the operator it would stop using that script and wrote the incident into the release record at 15:52.

That record says a hotfix was the only way to stop the rollout. The docs describe one more route. Per the "Halt a completed rollout" section of Google's APKs and Tracks guide, a completed release can be set to halted if the track already has an earlier published completed release; new users and existing users who update then get that earlier release. The completed release before 1.6.029 was vc94. We never tried this, so we do not know whether Play would have accepted it. What we did instead was add +1 day and +3 day stability rows to the monitoring doc. The late check on October 15 found no regression signal, though Play's crash numbers were out of reach because the reporting API lacked permissions.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Internal track first, then promote the same build

One rule was already two days old when this happened. On October 9, 1.6.026 went straight to 100% of production through the Publisher API, and the operator asked that next time the build go to internal testing first and be promoted from there. A sideloaded APK cannot show the Play path end to end: Play signing, billing, Play's automatic protection. The bundle is uploaded once, and production gets the same versionCode in a new edit.

1.6.029 did follow that order, but the fraction was lost in the second step, the promotion from internal to production. The two versions after it kept the fraction too.

VersionFirst production step100%Basis for the call
1.6.029 (vc97)Oct 11, completed (meant to be 20%)from the startlate check Oct 15: no regression signal, crash numbers not seen
1.6.030 (vc102 → vc103)Oct 17, inProgress 0.2Oct 18+1 day: zero crashes, no change to ad code
1.6.031 (vc105)Oct 18, inProgress 0.2Oct 19+1 day: zero crashes, zero failed checks

The 20% day for 1.6.030 did not collect enough real users to compare anything. Most of the 1.6.030 users in GA4 were Play pre-launch report test devices and our own development phones. So the 100% call rested on zero crashes and a diff showing no ad code had changed.

The promotion script now never reads the fraction by position

From 1.6.031 on, each version folder has its own release_production.py, and promotion goes through it. Trimmed to the core:

commit = '--commit' in sys.argv          # dry run unless given
fraction = float(sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--fraction') + 1]) if '--fraction' in sys.argv else 0.2
edit = call('POST', f'{API}/edits', {})['id']
done = False
try:
    internal = call('GET', f'{API}/edits/{edit}/tracks/internal')['releases']
    new = [r for r in internal if r.get('versionCodes') == [NEW]]
    if len(new) != 1:
        sys.exit(f'vc{NEW} is not on internal')
    prod = call('GET', f'{API}/edits/{edit}/tracks/production')['releases']
    old = [r for r in prod if r.get('versionCodes') == [OLD] and r['status'] == 'completed']
    if len(old) != 1:
        sys.exit(f'no completed vc{OLD} on production')
    call('PUT', f'{API}/edits/{edit}/tracks/production', {'track': 'production', 'releases': [
        {'versionCodes': [NEW], 'status': 'inProgress', 'userFraction': fraction, ...},
        old[0]]})
    call('POST', f'{API}/edits/{edit}:validate')
    if commit:
        call('POST', f'{API}/edits/{edit}:commit'); done = True
finally:
    if not done:
        call('DELETE', f'{API}/edits/{edit}')   # dry run or failure: throw the edit away

(The real script's messages are in Korean; they are translated here.) Four things changed:

  • status is hard-coded as inProgress. A missing fraction cannot fall through to completed, and the fraction only changes through the named --fraction flag.
  • The internal testing track must hold exactly one release with that versionCode. A promotion that skipped internal stops here.
  • Production must hold exactly one completed release of the previous version. That is what the other 80% keep getting while the new release sits at 20%.
  • The default is a dry run: it validates and then deletes the edit. The only run that changes anything is the one with --commit, after the operator has checked. 1.6.031 shipped that way on October 18, after the operator confirmed.

The PUT body has the same shape as the request that got the 403 on October 11: new release inProgress, previous release completed. For 1.6.031 the new release had not been served to anyone yet, and this request passed validate and commit.

The rule now, and a check not yet in code

If you give an agent permission to ship to production, do not let it use a script that takes the rollout fraction as a positional argument. Code that defaults to completed when the fraction is missing turns one slip into a full release. The rule now: uploads go to the internal testing track only, the operator installs from Play and checks, and then the same build is promoted. Promotion runs as a dry run first, sits at 20% of production for a day, and only then goes to 100%.

One line is still missing from the code. The project notes say to confirm, before commit, that the PUT response shows status inProgress and the right userFraction. The current script builds the PUT body itself and never reads the response. The next version of the script gets this check:

tr = call('PUT', f'{API}/edits/{edit}/tracks/production', body)
mine = [r for r in tr['releases'] if r.get('versionCodes') == [NEW]]
if len(mine) != 1 or mine[0]['status'] != 'inProgress' or mine[0].get('userFraction') != fraction:
    sys.exit(f'PUT response does not match: {mine}')   # stop before commit

We will also write down the halt procedure from the docs at the next staged release, and check then whether a stray completed could send new installs back to the previous version without waiting for a hotfix build. Our release checks, in order, are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app, and the app itself is on the SugarSpeller page.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Reworking a long-running spelling app: all 8 parts

  1. A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop
  2. 10,001 lines of greeting cards: built with an AI agent, removed with one

FAQ

Can a completed Play release be turned back into a staged rollout?

We could not do it. The PUT that set the completed vc97 to inProgress 0.2 was refused with 403 PERMISSION_DENIED. The documented option left is to halt the completed release when the track has an earlier completed release, which we did not try, so we do not know if it works.

How do you set userFraction in the Publisher API?

In edits.tracks, give the release status inProgress and a userFraction between 0 and 1 (0.2 for 20%), then commit the edit. userFraction can only be set while the status is inProgress or halted. Put the previous completed release in the same releases array so the remaining users keep getting it.

How do you take a staged rollout to 100%?

In a new edit, change the same release's status to completed and commit. SugarSpeller does this after one day at 20% of production with zero crashes and zero failed checks: October 18 for 1.6.030 and October 19 for 1.6.031.

Sources: the app's release records for 1.6.029 to 1.6.031, the command output from that day's release session, and the Google Play Developer API docs (edits.tracks updated 2026-09-28, APKs and Tracks updated 2025-12-18). Rechecked on October 21, 2026.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Play Console DEX optimization and an R8 keep rule – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used

A leftover Kakao SDK ProGuard file kept every public member of every class out of R8; deleting it moved the bundle's r8.json numbers from 39% to 85%.

Release-only bugs from R8 4/4

Google Play Console shows, as percentages, how much of an uploaded app bundle's code R8 has optimized, obfuscated and shrunk. When those numbers are low, the usual suspect is -dontoptimize, which switches optimization off. Our Korean spelling checker SugarSpeller had already dropped that line, yet on September 25, 2026 Play still rated its bundle "intermediate": optimization 36%, obfuscation 39%, shrinking 39%. The rest of the gap came from a keep-rule file for the Kakao SDK, which the app does not even use.

Deleting that file the same day moved the shrinking figure in the bundle's r8.json from 39% to 85%, and the AAB went from 18.4 MB to 11.6 MB. Below is how to read Play's figures from a local build before uploading, and the order in which we found the rule.

The Play Console figure is r8.json turned upside down

Those percentages line up with a file the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) already puts in every R8-processed release bundle: BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json. Its stats block records the share of code that was not shrunk, obfuscated or optimized.

unzip -p app-release.aab BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json
"stats":{"noObfuscationPercentage":61.48,
         "noOptimizationPercentage":64.27,
         "noShrinkingPercentage":61.47}

Subtract each value from 100 and you get what Play shows: 61.47 became 39% shrunk, 64.27 became 36% optimized. We matched that from our own before-and-after numbers, not from a Google spec, but it held for the two Play readings we have (0% before, 36/39/39% after the first fix). That lets you read the metric locally before uploading anything.

The build used AGP 9.4.0 with R8 full mode, resource shrinking and the stock proguard-android-optimize.txt. Our repository notes say Play wants this metric addressed by February 2027; we could not re-check the wording on the Play screen for this note.

Dropping -dontoptimize took optimization from 0% to 36%

A commit on September 20 removed -dontoptimize from the shared ProGuard file. It had been added on purpose, out of fear that optimization would break the Gson reflection that parses spelling results, and it pinned Play's optimization figure at 0%. The comparison baseline was the previous HEAD (1.6.019) built in the same environment.

Unoptimized code went from 100% to 64.25%, and uncompressed DEX from 16.31 MB to 14.84 MB. The AAB dropped from 29.95 MB to 18.33 MB, but most of that was a greeting-card editor and roughly 11 MB of its assets leaving in the same release. Optimization's own share sits inside the 1.5 MB of DEX.

Unobfuscated code rose from 54.16% to 61.46%. The commit put that down to "app code shrank, so the SDK keep rules weigh more" and moved on. Version 1.6.020 shipped on September 22. Three days later came the 36/39/39% reading from the top of this note.

The merged configuration.txt had a rule on class *

Every rule R8 actually applied ends up in one file, app/build/outputs/mapping/release/configuration.txt: the defaults, the app's six .pro files, and the consumer rules each library AAR brings along. The merged file from the October 9, 2026 release build is 1,369 lines, short enough to read end to end. Reading through it on September 25 turned up this block.

# Kakao SDK ProGuard file (in the repo since the first commit, 2020-12-16)
-keep class com.kakao.** { *; }
-keepattributes Signature
-keepclassmembers class * {
  public static <fields>;
  public *;
}
-dontwarn android.support.v4.**,org.slf4j.**,com.google.android.gms.**

In the third rule, class * has no condition, so it matches every class in the app and in every library. Their public fields and methods can then not be removed, renamed or inlined. And the Kakao SDK (the SDK for KakaoTalk login and sharing) was not a dependency at all; even its Maven repository line in the root build script was commented out.

The September 25 commit deleted the file and both build references to it, release and debug. It also deleted a Retrofit rule file that no build had ever referenced.

Do not ship an unconditional keep rule on class * in an Android app. Libraries that need rules already ship them as consumer rules inside their AAR.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Before and after: r8.json and sizes for both changes

Each pair of columns comes from a different day and a different commit, so compare within a pair. Even the same configuration drifts in the second decimal: 64.25% on September 20, 64.27% on September 25.

Metric1.6.019 baseline-dontoptimize removed (Sep 20)Before kakao file removal (Sep 25)After (Sep 25)
Not optimized100%64.25%64.27%15.68%
Not obfuscated54.16%61.46%61.48%15.14%
Not shrunknot recordednot recorded61.47%15.18%
As Play shows it (opt/obf/shrink)optimization 0% (Play screen)36/39/- (derived from r8.json)36/39/39% (Play screen)84/85/85 (derived from r8.json, not yet seen on Play)
DEX16.31 MB (uncompressed)14.84 MB15.6 MB (total)8.2 MB
AAB29.95 MB18.33 MB (asset removal included)18.4 MB11.6 MB

Measured by DEX size, deleting one rule did about five times what removing -dontoptimize did. DEX shrank by 1.5 MB on September 20 and by 7.4 MB (47%) on September 25, and the AAB lost another 6.8 MB.

Before release, a release APK signed with the debug key ran on an API 34 emulator. A spelling check against Naver (Korea's largest web portal) came back with the two corrections the server reported, and the post-check quiz bubble, the quiz screen and Remote Config content injection all worked. The five JSON key strings Gson reads were still present verbatim in the release DEX. (A headless emulator returns black screenshots, so we read screen text with uiautomator dump instead.)

From September 22 to October 3 the post-release watch log recorded zero crashes for 1.6.020, for 1.6.024 (the first release without the kakao rule) and for 1.6.025, and closed the item as "no regression".

The clue the agent explained away

An AI coding agent (Claude) wrote both commits. On September 20 it declared in the commit message that the -dontoptimize line was the cause. It also recorded, accurately, that unobfuscated code had gone up by more than 7 points. It did not check which rule was holding that code; it filled the gap with a guess that the keep rules had not changed and the SDKs simply weighed more.

On the afternoon of September 25 the operator pasted a Play Console screenshot, noted that the bundle still looked unoptimized, and asked for a deeper analysis. Only then did the agent open the merged configuration, and the seven-line file from 2020 surfaced. Opening configuration.txt first instead of guessing would have saved five days.

Two lines went into the repository's agent instructions afterwards: never add a keep rule on class *, and check the merged result in configuration.txt. The checks we run to catch release-only R8 failures before shipping are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Finding the same kind of rule in your app

  1. Pull r8.json out of the release AAB and subtract the three stats shares from 100. That previews Play's figures before you upload.
  2. Search the merged configuration.txt for unconditional class * rules: grep -n -A3 -E '^-keep(classmembers)? class \* ' app/build/outputs/mapping/release/configuration.txt
  3. For each hit, work out which SDK it was written for and check whether that SDK is still in your dependencies. If it is not, delete the whole rule file.
  4. Rebuild, compare r8.json and the DEX size, then run the release APK on a device or emulator and walk the paths that use reflection (Gson parsing, in our case).

Still open

  • Confirming the Play screen. The repository holds only the 85% derived from r8.json; nothing records the Play Console figure after release. We will capture it on the next upload.
  • The ratio creeping back. A new Firebase dependency in 1.6.025 pulled the build down about 5 points, to roughly 80%. The release AAB left on disk from October 9, 2026 reads 20.23% unoptimized with 9.30 MB of DEX (9,302,488 bytes). Next step: diff configuration.txt to see which consumer rule arrived.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Release-only bugs from R8: all 4 parts

  1. R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count

This is the last part.

FAQ

Does the Play Console DEX optimization warning block uploads?

It did not in September 2026: bundles at 0% and at 36% optimization both shipped normally. Our repository notes say Play expects it fixed by February 2027, so it is not something to leave for later.

Can I see the optimization percentage before uploading to Play?

Yes. Extract BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json from the release AAB and subtract the three stats values from 100. For this app, 61.47 matched Play's 39%. That mapping is our inference from repository records, and nothing yet records whether Play showed the 85% that 15.18 implies.

How do I find the keep rule that is holding the metric down?

Search the merged configuration.txt for -keep or -keepclassmembers rules on wide patterns such as class * or ** with no condition attached. Here it was a single -keepclassmembers class * { public *; } block in a file for an SDK the app did not use.

Sources: SugarMount's app repository (the September 20 and 25 commits, changelog entries for 1.6.020 and 1.6.023, the post-release watch log) and an r8.json read again from a local release AAB (checked October 20, 2026).

item.title: Accurate sitemap lastmod from a content hash – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash

Don't type lastmod by hand or copy it from git commit dates. Compute it from a hash of the page body, and keep the date itself out of what you hash.

Getting this site indexed 1/3

A sitemap's lastmod tells search engines which pages changed and are worth fetching again, so if every page carries the same date it tells them nothing. After one commit on October 18, 2026, all 51 URLs in this site's sitemap.xml said 2026-10-18. Today a page's modified date only moves when a hash of its body changes: a commit on October 19 touched 99 HTML files and moved the date on just 6 existing pages.

Commit dates made every page look new

The old build set each URL's lastmod to the date of the last git commit that touched the file. That helper arrived on October 5 in a commit that carries an AI coding agent's co-author line. The agent's code measured when a file changed.

It broke on the October 18 site-wide commit. Fifty-two HTML files went into one commit, each gaining an RSS <link> in its head, and the sitemap went from five different dates to all 51 URLs on that day. Re-running today's hash rule (the inside of <main>) over those 52 files, only 2 had real body changes: the SugarDoc app page in Korean and English. 42 had identical bodies. The other 8 differed by a single added line, a "last updated" date. (Counting structured data in the head as well, 11 pages changed their FAQ or feature list.)

Google's sitemap documentation says it uses lastmod only if the value is "consistently and verifiably" accurate, and gives a copyright date update as an example of a change that isn't significant.

The date moves only when the body hash changes

The restructure that evening moved all page dates into one JSON file. The agent co-wrote that commit too. The new dates module opens by citing the spec section that defines the rules. For a hand-written page it hashes the inside of <main> with breadcrumbs and build-generated blocks removed:

def hand_input(page_html):
    inner = main_html(page_html)       # inside <main> only
    inner = _CRUMBS_RE.sub("", inner)  # drop breadcrumbs
    inner = strip_build_blocks(inner)  # drop <!-- build:* --> blocks
    return _WS_RE.sub(" ", inner).strip()
# same hash: keep dates; new hash: modified = today
# new page: published = modified = today

The easy thing to miss is the date itself. In that site-wide commit the "last updated" line sat inside <main> as plain HTML. Hash that line and every date change looks like a content change, so the next day's build moves the date again, forever. On hand-written pages the line now lives in a build:meta block. Those 8 app pages became generated pages built from data/apps.json, so their hash covers the input data, not the HTML. A unit test (test_every_marker_block_is_removed) asserts the phrase never reaches the hash input, and test_idempotent_next_day checks that a rerun the next day leaves the dates alone.

Never derive lastmod from commit dates or build dates. Don't let people edit it either: the repository's AGENTS.md says "never edit dates by hand" (how we write that file is in How to write AGENTS.md).

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

99 files touched, 6 dates moved

One commit on October 19 touched 99 HTML files, mostly to bump a ?v= cache-busting value on the stylesheet links. Apart from 14 new pages, the modified date moved on 6 existing ones: the home page, the apps hub and the privacy policy list, in Korean and English, each of which now lists the new pages.

IndexNow pings (a protocol for telling Bing, Naver and others about changed URLs) follow the same dates. The ping script picks only pages whose modified date is today, and it is a dry run unless you pass --send.

If you want to try this

  1. Cut each page down to its body. Leave out breadcrumbs, blocks your build inserts and anything that changes on every build, such as a date line.
  2. Collapse whitespace and hash it. Same hash, keep the dates; new hash, set modified to today. A new page gets today as both published and modified.
  3. Keep dates and hashes in one file in the repository, and write down that nobody edits it by hand.
  4. Read sitemap lastmod, the date shown on the page and the IndexNow list from that one file.
  5. Make a commit that only changes a stylesheet URL and confirm that no page's date moves.

What we check next

The related-notes list (build:extra) is excluded from the hash. Google counts link changes as significant, yet when a new note joins that list, older notes keep their dates. We will decide after reading Search Console's crawl data in November 2026. On the old github.io property these sitemaps went unprocessed for ten days, so we could not even tell whether lastmod was being read; that story is in Search Console showed 'Couldn't fetch' for ten days.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Getting this site indexed: all 3 parts

  1. Search Console showed 'Couldn't fetch' for ten days; a new domain property processed the same sitemaps in seconds

FAQ

Does Google actually use sitemap lastmod?

Yes, but only when the values are consistently and verifiably accurate, for example when they match the page's real last change. The same page (updated 2026-07-08) says Google ignores priority and changefreq.

Do you send every URL to IndexNow on each deploy?

No. Only pages modified today go out. The full list (--all) is meant to be sent once, right after registering the site with Naver Search Advisor, the webmaster console of the Korean search engine Naver.

Sources: this site's git history and its date and IndexNow scripts (as of October 20, 2026).

item.title: CarDrawer (차서랍): used-car dealer app for Android – SugarMount
item.description:
CarDrawer 차서랍

Android app for used-car dealers in Korea

Recruiting 5 pilot shopsClosed testing on Google Play soon

One drawer
per car.

AI files every receipt and flags what's missing.

Snap a receipt, invoice or inspection report, or share a PDF. CarDrawer pulls out the vendor, amount, date and plate as suggestions and files them in that car's drawer. Every morning it shows what is due today, which papers are missing, which costs need approval and which cars have started losing money.

Apply for the pilot How it works

Free cost sheet template (CSV) · A per-car cost sheet that opens in Excel: 18 cost items with total-cost and difference formulas. No sign-up or email needed.

  • AI only suggests. A person confirms.
  • We never ask for your HeyDealer, Encar or other platform passwords.
  • Your costs are visible only to you and the people you allow.
The problem

Costs leak car by car, and papers scatter across chat rooms

Receipts in drawers and chats

Transport, polish, body work, dealer fees, listing ads: one car collects close to ten cost items. Matching each receipt to the right car falls on the office manager.

Deadlines in someone's head

Ownership transfer, inspection-report validity and platform claim windows differ for every car. Missing one means fines or disputes.

Profit known only after the sale

Financing interest and late invoices can turn a car you thought was profitable into a loss, and it is hard to see where each car stands today.

A car bought for ₩30.01M: about ₩630,000 left if sold in 3 months · cut the price in month 7 and it becomes a ₩970,000 loss

A dealer's public cost sheet (9 cost items; re-listing, interest and re-inspection added in month 7). Source: Clien post, 23 Aug 2025 (Korean), checked Oct 2026. One case, not a general figure.
What it does

Snap it, it sticks. Missing pieces come first.

  • Snap and it sticks

    “Snap the receipt. We attach it to the right car.”

    Upload from the camera, gallery or share menu in three taps. AI suggests the vendor, amount, date and plate; only values checked against the original reach your costs.

  • Today's deadlines, cars losing money

    “Do you know how much this car still makes?”

    The first screen gathers overdue tasks, today's deadlines, pending approvals and at-risk cars, with legal, platform and in-house deadlines labelled separately.

  • One shop, your costs stay yours

    “You decide who sees what.”

    Owner, buyers and office staff share the same car cards. Purchase prices, costs and counterparties are visible only with permission, and access ends the moment someone leaves.

  • Works next to your apps

    “Keep your apps. We fill the gaps.”

    Cars from any channel on one board. Platform screenshots are stored, never scraped. Export costs as CSV for your existing system or accountant.

Screens

Today · Review · Costs · Sales prep

Screen examples. All cars, plates, people and shop names are made up; the app is in development and may look different.

How it works

Upload → suggest → confirm → organise

  1. Upload on the lot. Buyers photograph receipts, invoices and inspection reports or share them. The app asks you to mask resident registration and similar ID numbers yourself with its masking tool before upload, and photo location data is removed on the device.
  2. AI suggests values. It sorts document types and copies vendor, amount, date and plate exactly as written. Fixed formulas, not AI, clean up and check the numbers.
  3. A person confirms against the original. Amounts, the car a document belongs to, odometer, accident or replacement marks and seizure or mortgage status always need human approval. The office can review in one batch later.
  4. Costs, deadlines and sales prep update. Confirmed values fill per-car costs and break-even, paperwork checklists, required ad items and draft descriptions.

“No information” is not “no problem”

Blank never means “none”. Every value carries a state, and anything not confirmed stays out of outgoing material.

  • Confirmed
  • AI suggestion
  • Needs review
  • Conflict
  • Unreadable
  • Not checked
  • Not entered
  • Confirmed absent
Open formulas

How costs and deadlines are calculated

Operating contribution

Sale income − purchase − direct costs − financing cost

Expected sale income₩22,300,000
Purchase− ₩20,000,000
Direct costs (body work, dealer fee, polish, ads, transport)− ₩1,330,000
Financing (₩20M · 12%/yr · 30 days, simple)− ₩197,260
Operating contribution₩772,740

Financing runs from the day funds were actually drawn, not the bid date. Overheads and tax are not included, so we never call it “net profit”. Demo figures.

Default deadline rules (reference)

TaskDefault reminder
Ownership transfer filing15 days by law; counting rules vary, so we remind at purchase date + 14 days
Inspection reportRe-inspection task after 120 days from the inspection date
Keeping report copies1 year from issue
Inspection warranty30 days or 2,000 km after delivery
Aged stockCaution at 60 days, warning at 90 (adjustable)

Reference settings based on Korean law and platform policies as checked in October 2026. Each rule is versioned and marked “dealer to confirm”; check before relying on it.

What it does not do

Things the app never does for you

  • Post listings, send messages, transfer money, bid or file documents. It prepares files and text and hands them to the share menu.
  • Connect to or scrape other platforms. Platform screenshots and auction diagnoses are stored only, never sent to AI.
  • Declare a car “accident-free” or write “warranty” or “lowest price” without evidence.
  • Perform statutory disclosure, inspections or ownership transfer. Those duties stay with the dealer.
  • Recommend purchase prices. The purchase-limit calculator only uses the assumptions you enter.
  • Give tax advice or file returns. It tags receipts and exports them.
Data and privacy

Customer data belongs to the dealership

  • For owner and buyer details in uploaded records, the dealership is the controller and we process them only as instructed. They are never used for marketing or AI training.
  • Data is stored in Google Cloud's Seoul region. Document reading uses Google Vertex AI (Gemini, paid tier), which may process outside Korea.
  • No advertising SDK or advertising ID. No payments inside the app.
  • Export everything as CSV and an original-file ZIP at any time, and for 30 days after you cancel.

Details: Privacy policy · Terms of service · Processors and sub-processors · Delete your account

We're looking for 5 pilot dealerships

For shops of 2 to 10 people that buy and resell their own stock. We visit Suwon and Gangseo (Seoul) dealer complexes first. Use it free for 4 weeks while we measure the time it saves together; if it saves none, you don't pay.

Apply for the pilot Pricing

Questions

Does it work on iPhone or a PC?

Android comes first. If pilot shops need review and cost screens on an office PC, we will add a web version based on the pilot results.

Does it sync with HeyDealer or Encar?

No. We don't take platform credentials or scrape anything. Screenshots or diagnosis files you upload are stored in the car's drawer and never sent to AI.

What if AI reads an amount wrong?

AI values stay marked “AI suggestion” until a person approves them against the original. Amounts and the car a document belongs to always need approval. Use “Report a problem” on any wrong result.

Can staff see each other's costs?

Purchase prices, costs, profit and counterparties are visible only with permission. Independent dealers sharing a shop name decide who sees their costs.

What happens to my data if I stop?

You can view and export (CSV, original-file ZIP) for 30 days after cancelling; then it is deleted. Cancel in the app or with one email.

How much does it cost?

The 14-day trial needs no card and never converts to paid automatically. See pricing.

Contact

For demos, onboarding or bug reports, email us with your shop name and how to reach you. We reply as soon as we can.

Email: sugarmount21@gmail.com

Package name
com.sugarmount.cardrawer
Developer
Simpest21 (Google Play developer name SugarMount)

Help articles

  • We're looking for 5 pilot dealerships
  • Pricing

Related apps

  • SugarSpeller
  • SugarClip
  • HWP Viewer SugarDoc
